ja-vi-elsker-dette-landet: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson wrote the words between 1859 and 1868, and his cousin Rikard Nordraak wrote the melody during the winter of 1863 to 1864. The song was first performed in public on 17 May 1864, in connection with the 50th anniversary of the constitution. Bjørnson wrote in a modified version of the Danish used in Norway at the time, and the text sung today keeps his words with modernised spelling and punctuation. Usually only the first and the last two verses are sung, the first by far the most often. In each verse the last two lines are sung twice, with one or two words repeated a further time.

Until the mid-1860s the songs Sønner av Norge and Norges Skaal were commonly regarded as national anthems, Sønner av Norge being the better known. Ja, vi elsker dette landet gradually came to be recognised as an anthem from the mid-1860s, and until the early 20th century both were used, with Sønner av Norge preferred in official situations. Norway had no official anthem until 11 December 2019.

The original version contained a verse that hailed the king, who had succeeded his father in July 1859. It described the king as a strong and open border guard whose best weapon was the brethren pact, a military treaty by which Norway, Sweden and Denmark were to help one another if any was attacked. When German troops invaded South Jutland in February 1864, none of the partners came to Denmark's rescue, and the failure shattered hopes of a united Scandinavia. Bjørnson went from monarchist to republican, and the tribute to the sovereign was struck from the song.

In 1905 the Norwegian Storting declared the union with Sweden dissolved on 7 June, which brought the two nations to the brink of war in the autumn. Swedish Social Democrats, whose leaders Hjalmar Branting and Zeth Höglund spoke for a peaceful settlement, sang the song to support the Norwegian right to leave the union. During the Second World War it was used both by the Norwegian resistance and by Nazi collaborators, mainly for propaganda, and the German occupiers eventually forbade any use of it.
Norway also has an unofficial royal anthem, Kongesangen, based on God Save the King, and the psalm Gud signe vårt dyre fedreland, by Elias Blix, which is often called the national psalm.
jabalpur: Jabalpur lies on the banks of the Narmada River and is the administrative headquarters of the Jabalpur district and division. Its name is traditionally derived from a sage named Jabali who meditated on the river's banks, though another theory takes it from the Arabic jabal, meaning boulders. The city is known for the Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat, a gorge of marble cut by the Narmada below the Dhuandhar Falls. In 1828 the British officer William Henry Sleeman found a dinosaur fossil near Bara Simla Hill, the first such find in Asia.

Ashokan relics from about 300 BCE at Rupnath, north of the city, indicate Mauryan presence. Later the region came under the Satavahana dynasty and then became a vassal state of the Gupta Empire. The Kalachuri dynasty conquered it in 875. Under the Gond kings of Garha-Mandla the city was an important centre of power: Madan Shah built a watchtower and small fort at Madan Mahal, and Rani Durgavati built more than 85 ponds. A Maratha invasion in 1742 made the kingdom a tributary, and the Maratha rulers of Sagar annexed it in 1781. The Bhonsle kings of Nagpur held the Narmada valley until 1818, when the East India Company seized it after the Battle of Sitabuldi.

The British made Jabalpur the headquarters of the Narmada territories, set up a cantonment and made it the capital of the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories, which joined the Central Provinces in 1861. The Congress session at nearby Tripuri in 1939 re-elected Subhas Chandra Bose as president against Mahatma Gandhi's candidate, and he resigned in April of that year. After independence in 1947 the Central Provinces and Berar became Madhya Pradesh.

Jabalpur is the seat of the Madhya Pradesh High Court and the zonal headquarters of the West Central Railway. Its municipal population was 1,081,677 at the 2011 census, and Hindi is the predominant language. Its cantonment is one of the largest in India, and ordnance factories, including the Gun Carriage Factory begun in 1904, make it a centre of defence industry. It is generally accepted that snooker originated here, devised in 1875 by Colonel Neville Chamberlain. The Hanumantal Bada Jain Mandir, a seventeenth-century temple with 22 shrines, is the largest independent Jain temple in India. The name Jubbulpore was replaced by Jabalpur in 2006.
jaca: Jaca stands on the Aragón River near the Pyrenees and the border with France, at a height of 820 metres. It lies at the crossing of two great early medieval routes, one from Toulouse to Santiago de Compostela and one from Pau to Zaragoza. The County and Kingdom of Aragon developed out of the city, and it was the capital of the district of Jacetania.

The origins of the city are obscure, but its name apparently derives from the Iacetani, whom Strabo lists among the small tribes of the Ebro basin. Jaca minted coins from the second half of the 2nd century BCE, showing a horseman with a spear and the Iberian inscription iaka. The Roman consul Cato the Elder began the conquest of the city in 195 BCE and finished it in the spring of 194 BCE. Huesca fell to the Muslims in 720, and the region of Jacetania then served as a buffer zone for the Carolingian Empire; by 799 Aureolo had stabilised an independent county.

Ramiro I of Aragon, who reigned from 1035 to 1063, gave it the title of city and capital of the Kingdom of Aragon, and in 1063 it was the site of the Synod of Jaca. As the Aragonese conquered land to the south from Muslim rule, the capital was moved to Huesca in 1096, though Jaca remained a market city for its region. It was home to Aragon's oldest Jewish community until the expulsion of 1492. In 1592 Philip II ordered the pentagonal citadel, designed by the Italian engineer Tibúrcio Spannocchi, to defend the Pyrenees against a possible French invasion. A mutiny there on 12 and 13 December 1930, whose leaders demanded the abolition of the monarchy, was suppressed with some difficulty.

Jaca has medieval walls and towers around the 11th-century Romanesque cathedral, and the citadel of the late 16th century. The Diocesan Museum of Jaca keeps Romanesque and Gothic frescoes from the district. From the early 1970s the town changed from a small garrison town into the gateway to winter resorts such as Astún and Candanchú.
jacobin-club: The club began in 1789 as the Club Breton, a group of Breton deputies at the Estates General at Versailles, and deputies from other regions soon joined. Early members included the comte de Mirabeau, the Abbé Sieyès, Antoine Barnave and Robespierre. It was re-founded in November 1789 and rented the refectory of the Dominican monastery of the Jacobins in the Rue Saint-Honoré, next to the Assembly. In January 1790 it took the name Société des amis de la Constitution, though its opponents had already dubbed it the Jacobins.

Once in Paris the club admitted citizens besides deputies. There were one hundred and fifty-two affiliated clubs by August 1790 and, at the peak, at least 7,000 chapters with a membership estimated at half a million or more. Women were not members but could follow debates from the balconies, and the high subscription confined membership to well-off men.

The club supported the monarchy until the eve of the Republic on 20 September 1792. In late 1791 a group around Brissot, later called Girondins, urged war with Prussia and Austria, which Robespierre opposed in the club; the war was decided in April 1792, and the two groups then polarised. On 2 June 1793 a crowd of armed men besieged the Convention, which expelled 22 leading Girondins. Robespierre and the Mountain then dominated the government until July 1794. In October 1793 twenty-one Girondins were sentenced to death, and between September 1793 and July 1794 there were 17,000 death sentences across France.

On 28 July 1794 the Convention had Robespierre and 21 associates guillotined. The club's membership fell to about 600, and gangs of the jeunesse dorée attacked it. On 12 November 1794 the National Convention decreed its permanent closure by a nearly unanimous vote, and within a year 93 percent of the Jacobin clubs had closed. An attempt to revive it in July 1799, the Club du Manège, was suppressed after about a month.

In power the Jacobins completed the abolition of feudalism, decided in principle on 4 August 1789 but held back by a clause requiring compensation. They set up the Cult of Reason and the Cult of the Supreme Being in place of Catholicism. They consolidated republicanism in France, while their unjudicial methods discredited the Revolution in many eyes. The term Jacobin was later applied to radicals of similar views.
jacques-cartier: Jacques Cartier was born on 31 December 1491 in Saint-Malo, the port on the north-east coast of Brittany. A respected mariner, he improved his social standing in 1520 by marrying Mary Catherine des Granches, a member of a leading aristocratic family. In 1534 Jean Le Veneur, bishop of Saint-Malo, introduced him to King Francis I, citing voyages to Newfoundland and Brazil as proof of his ability to lead ships to new lands.

Cartier sailed on 20 April 1534 under a royal commission, hoping to find a western passage to the East Indies. He explored the coasts of Newfoundland, the Gaspé and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and on 24 July planted a 10-metre cross in Gaspé Bay to claim the land for France. There he kidnapped the two sons of the St. Lawrence Iroquoian chief Donnacona, who agreed on condition that they return with European goods.

On a second voyage in 1535 he sailed up the St. Lawrence with three ships and 110 men to Stadacona, and on 2 October reached Hochelaga, now Montreal, where over a thousand people greeted the French. The rapids blocked his way; convinced that the river was the Northwest Passage, he named them the Lachine Rapids after the French word for China. The fleet wintered frozen at the mouth of the St. Charles River, and scurvy killed about 50 Iroquoians. A remedy from the tree annedda, learned from Domagaya, saved 85 of the French. Cartier then took Donnacona to France to tell of the Kingdom of Saguenay, said to hold gold and rubies.

In 1541 Jean-François de La Rocque de Roberval was named lieutenant general of the colonisation project, with Cartier as chief navigator. Cartier sailed ahead with five ships and settled at Cap-Rouge, founding the fortified Charlesbourg-Royal. The minerals he took to be diamonds and gold proved to be quartz and iron pyrites. Iroquoians reportedly killed about 35 settlers during the winter, and he returned to France in 1542; the settlement was abandoned in 1543.

Cartier spent his last years in Saint-Malo and on his nearby estate, and died on 1 September 1557 at the age of 65 during an epidemic, possibly of typhus, and was buried in Saint-Malo Cathedral. He was the first European to describe and map the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the St. Lawrence River, and the first to document the name Canada, which comes from the Iroquoian word kanata, meaning village. Eastern parts of the continent had been visited before him by the Norse and by Basque, Galician and Breton fishermen, and no permanent European settlement followed before 1605.
jaffa: Ancient Jaffa stood on a ridge of kurkar sandstone 40 metres high with a broad view of the coastline, which gave it strategic importance. The tell formed by the debris of centuries made the hill higher still. The name appears in Egyptian sources and the Amarna letters as Yapu. A tradition says it was named for Japheth, son of Noah, and Greek tradition links it with Andromeda's mother Iopeia; an outcrop of rocks near the harbour is said to be where Perseus rescued Andromeda.

Pottery shows that Jaffa was settled as early as the 4th millennium BCE, and its earliest settlement remains date to the 18th century BCE, when it was a small fortified site of about three hectares on the sea routes linking the Levant, Egypt and Cyprus. In the 15th century BCE it came under Egypt's New Kingdom and is listed among the cities conquered by Thutmose III. The Hebrew Bible calls it the northernmost Philistine city, the port through which cedars of Lebanon reached the Temple, and the place where the prophet Jonah embarked. Under Persian rule it was awarded to Sidon, as an inscription on the Sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II attests.

In the Hellenistic period Antigonus Monophthalmus captured it in 315 BCE and Ptolemy I Soter destroyed it in 312 BCE, but it was resettled and became a Ptolemaic mint. It passed to Seleucid control after the Battle of Paneas in 198 BCE. In the Roman period Pompey annexed it to Syria, Julius Caesar restored it to Judaea, and Herod captured it in 39 BCE, though the harbour Herod built at Caesarea reduced its importance. In the New Testament it is the town where Saint Peter raised the widow Dorcas and had the vision that led him to preach to the gentiles.

In the Crusades Jaffa was the centre of the County of Jaffa and Ascalon. The Battle of Jaffa of 1192 was followed by a truce between Richard the Lionheart and Saladin. Napoleon sacked the town in 1799, and the British took it in 1917. In the 19th century it became known for its orchards and the Jaffa orange.

Jaffa is the southern part of Tel Aviv-Yafo, to which it was united as a single municipality in 1950. Most of its Arab population fled or was expelled after the 1948 Palestine War, and it is one of the mixed cities of Israel. Before 1948 it had been a centre of Palestinian journalism, where the newspapers Falastin and Al-Difa' were founded.
jaffna: Excavations point to early settlement on the peninsula. A bronze seal from Anaikoddai carries Tamil-Brahmi and Indus script, and urn burials and inscribed potsherds have been found at Kandarodai, Poonakari and Anaikoddai. Finds at the fort show trade with South Asia, Arabia and the Far East. The region was part of the chiefdom of Naga Nadu, named in the Tamil epic Manimekalai and the Pali Mahavamsa, whose Naga people scholars think were assimilated to Tamil language and culture by the 9th century CE.

The name is Tamil, Yazhpanam, earlier Yazhpanapattinam, with a suffix meaning seaport. A legend tells that a king presented a sandy plain to a blind musician who played the yal, a stringed instrument.

In the 13th century the Kingdom of Aryacakravarti arose as an ally of the Pandyan Empire, with its capital at Nallur, now a suburb of Jaffna. Its rulers made it independent, and other regional kingdoms paid it tribute in the 13th and 14th centuries. It lost its independence to the Kotte Kingdom from 1450 to 1467 but was re-established.

In 1619 a Portuguese expedition led by Filipe de Oliveira captured Cankili II, the last native king, and moved control from Nallur to Jaffnapatao, a fortified town. The Dutch East India Company took it in 1658 after a three-month siege, rebuilt the fort and most of the Hindu temples the Portuguese had destroyed. Britain took over from 1796 and built roads and a railway to Colombo, while missionary societies founded the schools behind the town's high literacy.

After independence in 1948 relations between Sinhalese and Tamils worsened, and Jaffna became a centre of Tamil nationalism. The Jaffna library was burnt in 1981 and civil war began in 1983. The Sri Lankan Army regained the city in 1995, and the war ended in 2009. Jaffna is the capital of the Northern Province, about 396 kilometres from Colombo, on a flat limestone peninsula; most of its people are Sri Lankan Tamils, mainly Shaivite Hindus.
jagiellonian-university: Casimir III the Great concluded that Poland needed an educated class, above all lawyers who could arrange the country's laws and run its courts and offices. Pope Urban V allowed him to set up a university in Kraków, and a royal charter of foundation was issued on 12 May 1364, with a matching document from the city council granting privileges to the Studium Generale. After Casimir's death development stalled.

The university was restored in the 1390s. Queen Jadwiga and her husband Władysław II Jagiełło chose to buy an existing building rather than build, and in 1399 acquired a house on Żydowska Street that had belonged to the Pęcherz family. The queen gave all her personal jewellery to the university, which allowed it to enrol 203 students. On 26 July 1400 Jagiełło reformed it on the model of the Sorbonne, and a Faculty of Theology was established.

For several centuries almost the whole intellectual elite of Poland studied there. Its astronomers, lawyers and theologians attracted eminent scholars, among them Albert Brudzewski, who from 1491 to 1495 was one of Nicolaus Copernicus's teachers. It was the first university in Europe to set up independent chairs in mathematics and astronomy. Its golden age fell in the Polish Renaissance, between 1500 and 1535, when 3,215 students attended in the first decade of the 16th century. That record was not passed until the late 18th century.

After the third partition of Poland in 1795 Kraków became a free city under Austrian protection, and in 1846, after the Kraków Uprising, it passed to the Austrian Empire. The Austrians were in many ways hostile to the university but Ferdinand I of Austria decreed that it be kept. On 6 November 1939, after the German invasion, 184 professors were arrested and deported to Sachsenhausen concentration camp, and the university was closed for the rest of the war. It reopened in 1945, but was suppressed by the Communist government in 1954.

The Jagiellonian Library, which holds Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, has almost 6.5 million volumes.  The university's alumni include Copernicus, King John III Sobieski and Pope John Paul II,. Today it is a public research university whose grounds form part of the Kraków Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
jahangir: Prince Salim was born at Fatehpur Sikri on 31 August 1569, the third and only surviving son of Akbar and Maryam uz-Zamani. His two elder brothers, the twins Hassan Mirza and Hussain Mirza, had died in infancy, and Akbar sought the blessing of the religious leader Salim Chishti, who lived at Fatehpur Sikri. Salim studied Chagatai, Persian and Hindustani as well as military tactics.

In 1594 he led an army against a revolt of the Bundela at Orchha, and after their leader Vir Singh Deo surrendered, Orchha became a vassal state. In 1599, while Akbar was campaigning in the Deccan, Salim declared himself emperor at Allahabad and issued coins in his own name. The rebellion ended without a decisive battle, and by 1604 peace was restored through the mediation of nobles such as Man Singh of Amber.

Jahangir succeeded to the throne on 3 November 1605. In April 1606 his son Khusrau rebelled, left Agra with 350 horsemen and besieged Lahore, but Jahangir relieved the city and defeated him at Bhairowal. Khusrau was captured while crossing the Chenab, and Jahangir had his young aristocratic supporters tortured and impaled as a warning. Khusrau was later blinded and imprisoned until 1619.

From his marriage to Mehr-un-Nissa, later Empress Nur Jahan, Jahangir left the reins of government largely in her hands and appointed her relatives to high positions, which displeased courtiers and foreigners. He was famed for his Chain of Justice, by which subjects denied justice could appeal to the emperor, and he ordered the foundation of free hospitals in the cities of his empire. He recorded his reign and the natural world in his memoir, and commissioned painters such as Ustad Mansur to illustrate it. The editor Henry Beveridge, however, judged him a weak ruler who lost Qandahar to the Persians.

A lifelong user of opium and wine, Jahangir was frequently ill in the 1620s. He died in October 1627 near Bhimber, on the journey from Kashmir to Lahore. His entrails were buried at Baghsar Fort, and his body was taken to Lahore and buried at Shahdara Bagh, where his son Shah Jahan commissioned his tomb. Shah Jahan succeeded him after a brief succession crisis. The tomb site was placed on the tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage status in 1993.
jainism: Jainism is an ancient Indian religion rooted in the independent Śramaṇa tradition of ascetics, which developed alongside but distinct from the orthodox Vedic religion. Jains maintain that their faith is eternal and that in the present cosmic time cycle it has been guided by 24 tirthankaras, beginning with Rishabhanatha. Historians date the 23rd, Pārśvanātha, to about the eighth or seventh century BCE. The 24th, Mahavira, was a contemporary of the Buddha and a central figure in the Śramaṇa movement of Greater Magadha, which rejected the authority of the Vedas.

Some scholars have proposed that seals from the Indus Valley Civilization show early forms of Jain asceticism, but because the Indus script is undeciphered, mainstream historians treat this as a hypothesis. The Hathigumpha Inscription of King Kharavela of Kalinga at the Udayagiri Caves in Odisha, from the second century BCE, records his patronage of Jain monks.

Jainism teaches a path to spiritual purity through disciplined nonviolence, ahimsa, to all living creatures. It is transtheistic: the universe was not created and has no creator, governor, judge or destroyer. Its philosophy rests on three ethical pillars, ahimsa, anekantavada, the doctrine that reality has many sides and no single viewpoint is completely true, and aparigraha, non-possession. Purification of the soul and liberation, moksha, are held to be achievable through the three jewels of right vision, right knowledge and right conduct. Laypersons keep five small vows and mendicants five great vows. Nonviolence led the community to avoid agriculture and warfare, and many Jains became merchants and bankers.

Devout Jains practise lacto-vegetarianism, and monks and nuns and some followers avoid root vegetables, since tiny organisms are injured when the plant is pulled up. The most fundamental invocation, accepted by all sects, is the Namokar Mantra. The most important annual festival is Paryushana among the Śvētāmbaras and Dasa lakshana parva among the Digambaras, a time of fasting and prayer.

The community is divided into the Digambara (sky-clad) and Śvētāmbara (white-clad) traditions, which differ on monastic discipline, canonical texts and the liberation of women. The Digambara account places the origin of the schism around the fourth century BCE, when Bhadrabahu predicted a twelve-year famine in Magadha and led monks to Karnataka. Most modern scholars, such as Padmanabh Jaini and Paul Dundas, conclude that it was a gradual hardening of differences over several centuries.

Royal patronage helped Jainism grow and decline. Rashtrakuta kings sponsored major Jain cave temples, and the Yadava dynasty built many temples at the Ellora Caves between 700 and 1000 CE. The Pallava king Mahendravarman I converted from Jainism to Shaivism. Virchand Gandhi, a Gujarati Jain scholar, represented Jainism at the first World Parliament of Religions in 1893 in Chicago. Jainism has between four and five million followers, mostly in India.
jaipur: Jaipur lies in eastern Rajasthan, 268 km from New Delhi, and covers 467 km2. Fertile alluvial plains lie to the east and south, while the northern and western margins have hill chains and arid areas; the Aravalli range bounds the city, with the Nahargarh hills to the north and the Jhalana hills to the east. The Dravyavati River serves as the main drainage channel. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with rain falling mostly in July and August with the southwest monsoon.

Jai Singh II, the Kachhwaha Rajput ruler of Amer, who ruled from 1699 to 1743, founded Jaipur on 18 November 1727 and gave it his name. He planned to move his capital 11 km from Amer because of a growing population and increasing water scarcity, and the city was planned on the principles of Vastu Shastra and Shilpa Shastra under the guidance of Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. Construction began in 1726. The city had gates facing east, west and north, and its architecture was heavily influenced by the 17th-century architectural renaissance under Mughal rule.

In 1876 the city was painted pink to welcome Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, which gave it the epithet Pink City. In the British period it was the capital of the princely state of Jaipur. In the 19th century it grew rapidly, reaching 160,000 people by 1900, and after independence in 1947 it became the capital of the new state of Rajasthan in 1949.

Jaipur is the capital and largest city of Rajasthan, with 3,046,163 people at the 2011 census, and Hindi is the official language. The earlier rulers invited skilled artisans from India and abroad, and the city remains known for block printing, stone carving, jewellery, gems, blue pottery and hand-knotted rugs. Its sites include the City Palace, Hawa Mahal, Amer Fort and the Jantar Mantar observatory, a collection of 19 astronomical instruments. The Jantar Mantar was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2010, and the historic city centre on 6 July 2019.
jakarta: Jakarta lies on the north-western coast of Java at the mouth of the Ciliwung river, facing Jakarta Bay. It covers about 664 square kilometres of land. Apart from some hills in the south, the city spreads across low, flat terrain, much of it an alluvial plain with elevations from below sea level to about 50 metres. Thirteen rivers run through it toward the bay. The plain was historically swampy, and seasonal flooding remains common.

The Buni culture, a prehistoric pottery culture of the northern and western coast of Java, is dated to roughly 400 BCE to 100 CE. The mid-5th-century Tugu inscription, found near Tanjung Priok, records the excavation of two waterways and attributes one of them to King Purnawarman. By the 10th century the Sunda Kingdom ruled the area, and by the early 16th century Kalapa was one of its leading ports. The Portuguese writer Tomé Pires called it Sunda's most important trading port, drawing ships from Sumatra, Malacca and Java. A treaty of 21 August 1522 allowed the Portuguese to build a fortress at Kalapa.

In 1527 Islamic forces captured Kalapa, and sources differ over whether Fatahillah or Sunan Gunung Jati led them. The settlement became a dependency of the Banten Sultanate under the name Jayakarta. The Dutch East India Company seized and destroyed Jayakarta in 1619 and rebuilt it as Batavia, its main administrative centre in Asia and an important trading port. In the early 19th century the Dutch colonial administration moved south to Weltevreden.

Indonesian independence was proclaimed in Jakarta in 1945, and after the Indonesian National Revolution it became the capital of the unitary republic in 1950. It became a first-level region in 1957 and a Special Capital Region in 1961. In 2022 the Indonesian government began the legal process of moving the capital to Nusantara in East Kalimantan.

Jakarta is the capital and largest city of Indonesia, with the status of a province, and had about 11 million registered residents in 2025. No ethnic group forms a majority; Javanese, Betawi, Sundanese and Chinese Indonesians are the largest. The Betawi people formed in colonial Batavia from people of varied origins. Indonesian is the official language, and the city hosts the headquarters of ASEAN. Its Old Town keeps the historic core.
jalisco: The name comes from the Nahuatl xalisco, meaning over a sandy surface, and until about 1836 it was spelled Xalisco. Nomadic peoples moving south arrived in the area around 15,000 years ago, and some of the oldest evidence of human occupation is found around Lake Zacoalco and Lake Chapala. When the Spanish arrived the main ethnic groups were the Cazcanes in the north, the Huichols in the north-west, the Guachichil in the Los Altos area, the Cuyutecos, who spoke Nahuatl, in the west, and the Tecuexes and Cocas near what is now Guadalajara.

At the start of the 19th century the Intendencia of Guadalajara still included Colima, parts of Zacatecas and the San Blas region. The area had relative freedom from Spanish colonial authorities and prospered with fewer trade restrictions, which, together with indigenous resentment of Spanish rule dating from the 16th century, made it sympathetic to the insurgent movements of the early 19th century.

Jalisco is a state in western Mexico with 342 kilometres of Pacific coastline, bordered by Nayarit, Zacatecas, Aguascalientes, Guanajuato, Michoacán and Colima. The saying Jalisco es México reflects how many things typically associated with Mexico originated there, among them mariachi, charreadas, the Mexican Hat Dance, tequila and the wide-brimmed sombrero. Mariachi is thought to have originated in the town of Cocula, and the music became most developed around Guadalajara.

Jalisco has 125 municipalities, and its capital and largest city is Guadalajara. The 2020 census counted 8,348,151 people, over half of them in the Guadalajara metropolitan area. The Huichols and the Nahuas are its two significant indigenous populations. Tequila is made from the blue agave of a small region of the state, and José Antonio Cuervo received the first official permission to make and sell it in 1758. San Juan de los Lagos, where an image of the Virgin Mary made in the 16th century is venerated, is one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in Mexico.
jamaica: Jamaica covers 10,991 square kilometres and is the third-largest island in the Greater Antilles and the Caribbean, after Cuba and Hispaniola. It lies about 145 km south of Cuba and 191 km west of Hispaniola. Mountains dominate the interior, among them the Blue Mountains in the east, where Blue Mountain Peak rises to 2,256 metres, and a narrow coastal plain surrounds them. The island lies within the main development region for Atlantic tropical cyclones and sometimes suffers heavy storm damage. When the Spanish arrived in 1494 the country was deeply forested, and European settlers later cleared much of it for timber and cultivation.

There is no archaeological evidence of human presence until about 500 CE. A group known as the Redware people, after their pottery, arrived around 600 CE, followed by the Taíno around 800 CE, who most likely came from South America. The Taíno lived by farming and fishing, and at their height are thought to have numbered some 60,000 people in around 200 villages headed by caciques. Christopher Columbus claimed the island for Spain after landing in 1494 on his second voyage. The first Spanish settlement, Sevilla, was founded in 1509 by Juan de Esquivel and abandoned around 1524; the capital moved to Spanish Town, then St. Jago de la Vega, around 1534.

The Taíno died in large numbers from introduced diseases and from enslavement by the Spanish, who then imported enslaved Africans. Many escaped and formed autonomous communities in the remote interior, mixing with the remaining Taíno; these became the Jamaican Maroons, who kept their freedom for generations under leaders such as Juan de Serras. By the early 17th century an estimated 2,500 to 3,000 people lived on the island.

England conquered Jamaica from Spain in 1655. Under British rule it became a leading sugar exporter, with a plantation economy that depended on importing enslaved Africans. The British emancipated all slaves in 1838, and many freedmen chose subsistence farms over plantation work. From the 1840s the British brought Chinese and Indian indentured labourers. Independence from the United Kingdom came on 6 August 1962.

Jamaica is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a Commonwealth realm, with a bicameral Parliament, and its constitution dates from 1962. The capital and largest city is Kingston. Most Jamaicans are of African or partly African descent, with minorities of European, Indian, Chinese and Lebanese origin. The Maroon communities of Accompong and elsewhere continue to keep their own traditions. The island is the birthplace of the Rastafari religion and of reggae, ska, dub and dancehall music, and its national motto is Out of Many One People.
james-bond: Ian Fleming began writing the first Bond novel, Casino Royale, on 17 February 1952 at his Goldeneye estate in Oracabessa, Jamaica, where he wrote all his Bond books during the months of January and February each year. Jonathan Cape, who did not like the manuscript as much as Fleming's friend William Plomer did, published it in 1953 on the recommendation of Fleming's older brother Peter, an established travel writer. Between 1953 and 1966 twelve novels and two short-story collections appeared, the last two books posthumously.

Bond is an officer of the Secret Intelligence Service, commonly known as MI6, and a Royal Naval Reserve Commander, known by his code number 007. Fleming said he was a compound of all the secret agents and commando types met during the war, among them his brother Peter. For the first five novels Bond carried a Beretta, until the gun expert Geoffrey Boothroyd wrote to Fleming that it was a lady's gun and suggested a Walther PPK; Fleming then named the armourer of MI6 Major Boothroyd. The films added gadgets from Q Branch, which became one of the motifs of the series.

After Fleming's death in 1964 other authors wrote authorised Bond novels, among them Kingsley Amis, John Gardner and Sebastian Faulks. The character has also been adapted for television, radio, comic strips and video games. CBS aired a live one-hour adaptation of Casino Royale on 21 October 1954, in which Barry Nelson played an American Bond.

Eon Productions, owned by Harry Saltzman and Albert R. Broccoli, released Dr. No in 1962 with Sean Connery as 007. The role passed to George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and, from Casino Royale in 2006, Daniel Craig, whose fifth and final film, No Time to Die, appeared in 2021. After Dr. No other studios rushed out imitations, 22 secret agent films in 1966 alone, and Bond was parodied in Carry On Spying (1964) and later the Austin Powers series. The Harry Palmer films, beginning with The Ipcress File (1965), were seen as an anti-Bond. Critics have accused the series of sexism and imperial nostalgia.
james-clerk-maxwell: James Clerk Maxwell was born on 13 June 1831 at 14 India Street, Edinburgh, the son of John Clerk Maxwell of Middlebie, an advocate, and Frances Cay. His mother took charge of his early education, and at eight he could recite long passages of John Milton and the whole of the 119th psalm. She died of abdominal cancer in December 1839. On 12 February 1842 his father took him to Robert Davidson's demonstration of electric propulsion and magnetic force. He studied at the University of Edinburgh from 1847 and discovered photoelasticity there. In October 1850 he went to Cambridge and graduated in 1854 from Trinity.

In 1856 Maxwell became head of the department of natural philosophy at Marischal College in Aberdeen. He studied the rings of Saturn and correctly proposed that they were made of numerous small particles, for which he won the Adams Prize in 1859. At King's College London, from 1860 to 1865, he did what was probably the most productive work of his career: he won the Rumford Medal in 1860 for his work on colour, was elected to the Royal Society in 1861. Around 1862 he calculated that an electromagnetic field travels at about the speed of light, and his paper A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field of 1865 showed that electric and magnetic fields travel through space as waves.

He also worked on the kinetic theory of gases, first deriving the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. In 1871 he came back to Cambridge as the first Cavendish Professor of Physics and oversaw the construction of the Cavendish Laboratory.

In April 1879 Maxwell began to have difficulty swallowing, the first symptom of his fatal illness. He died in Cambridge of abdominal cancer on 5 November 1879, aged 48, the same age and of the same type of cancer as his mother. Albert Einstein described his work on the centenary of Maxwell's birth as the most profound and fruitful that physics had experienced since the time of Newton, and when told in 1922 that he stood on Newton's shoulders he replied that he stood on those of Maxwell.
james-cook: James Cook was born on 7 November 1728 in the village of Marton in the North Riding of Yorkshire, the second of eight children of a Scottish farm labourer. His father's employer paid for him to attend a school run by a charitable foundation, and after five years of schooling he began working for his father, by then a farm manager. On 17 June 1755 he enlisted in the Royal Navy at Wapping. In the Seven Years' War he took part in the capture of the Fortress of Louisbourg in 1758 and surveyed the entrance to the St. Lawrence River, then spent five seasons charting the coast of Newfoundland. This work brought him to the attention of the Admiralty and the Royal Society.

Cook's first voyage, in HMS Endeavour from 1768 to 1771, was sponsored jointly by the Royal Navy and the Royal Society. Its stated purpose was to observe the 1769 transit of Venus from Tahiti, and secret orders told him to search for the supposed southern continent, Terra Australis, and to claim lands for Britain. In October 1769 he landed at Poverty Bay in New Zealand and, with the aid of the Tahitian priest Tupaia, was the first European to communicate with the Māori, though early encounters turned violent and several Māori were shot dead. On 19 April 1770 the crew sighted Point Hicks, the first European encounter with Australia's eastern coast.

On the second voyage, from 1772 to 1775, his crews became on 17 January 1773 the first recorded Europeans to cross the Antarctic Circle, though Cook never sighted Antarctica. He concluded that no polar landmass reached beyond about 50°S. The third voyage, from 1776, sought a North-West Passage; Cook visited Kerguelen Island and Hawaii and explored the coast of North America to the Bering Strait. He is credited with early work on preventing scurvy, and the Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal.

Cook returned to Hawaii in late November 1778 and landed at Kealakekua Bay on Hawaiʻi Island, where King Kalaniʻōpuʻu received him with respect. Many Hawaiians appear to have thought him an embodiment of the god Lono. After the ships left, a gale broke Resolution's foremast and they returned for repairs. Relations had worsened, and on 13 February 1779 Hawaiians stole one of his cutters. Cook was killed the next day. His voyages greatly expanded European knowledge of the Pacific. Historians debate his responsibility for violent encounters with Indigenous peoples, for the spread of infectious diseases and for claiming lands without consent.
james-frazer: Frazer was born on 1 January 1854 in Glasgow, the son of Katherine Brown and Daniel F. Frazer, a chemist. He studied at the University of Glasgow and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he graduated with honours in classics and remained a Classics Fellow all his life. He went on to study law at the Middle Temple but never practised. He was knighted in 1914. In 1896 he married Elizabeth Grove, known as Lilly, a writer who became his manager and publicist and arranged translations of his work into French.

Frazer's interest in social anthropology was aroused by E. B. Tylor's Primitive Culture of 1871 and encouraged by his friend, the biblical scholar William Robertson Smith. Except for visits to Italy and Greece he did not travel widely; his data came from ancient histories and from questionnaires mailed to missionaries and imperial officials around the world. He was the first scholar to describe in detail the relations between myths and rituals.

The Golden Bough appeared in two volumes in 1890, in three in 1900, and in a third edition of twelve volumes finished in 1915, with a thirteenth added in 1936. Lilly Frazer compiled an abridgement in 1922. In the third edition Frazer proposed that cultures pass from magic to religion to science. He saw magic and science as alike in their stress on experiment, and religion as belief in personal supernatural forces that are to be appeased. He also wrote a six-volume commentary on Pausanias's description of Greece, which scholars still value.

The Golden Bough reached beyond academia. Sigmund Freud cited Frazer's Totemism and Exogamy in Totem and Taboo, and the cycle of life, death and rebirth that Frazer saw behind many peoples' myths captivated artists and poets; the most notable product was T. S. Eliot's poem The Waste Land of 1922. Frazer's vision of the annual sacrifice of a Year-King has not been borne out by field studies.

Late-20th-century scholars criticised the work. Edmund Leach objected to its comparisons between widely separated cultures, and the historian Timothy Larsen argued that Frazer applied Christian terms such as baptism to non-Christian cultures. More recently the book has been criticised for assuming that European peasants, Aboriginal Australians and Africans represented earlier stages of cultural evolution. Frazer and his wife died in Cambridge within a few hours of each other on 7 May 1941.
james-ii-of-england: James was born on 14 October 1633 at St James's Palace, the second surviving son of Charles I and Henrietta Maria of France, and was designated Duke of York at birth. At the age of three he was appointed Lord High Admiral, an honorary post that became a substantive office after the Restoration. He was present at the Battle of Edgehill in October 1642 and spent most of the next four years in the Royalist capital of Oxford.

After the Restoration of 1660 he was created Duke of Albany in Scotland and was confirmed as Lord High Admiral. In October 1660 Charles II made him Governor of the Royal Adventurers into Africa, the company later reformed as the Royal African Company, which over its lifetime carried more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other single institution.

The Exclusion Crisis of 1679–81, when the Whigs tried to bar him from the succession, failed because the memory of the Commonwealth made the public reluctant to undermine hereditary succession. Charles II died on 6 February 1685, and James succeeded with widespread support, many believing that a Catholic monarchy would be temporary. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1685.

He enlarged the standing army and used his dispensing power to let Roman Catholics command regiments without taking the oath required by the Test Act. When Parliament objected he prorogued it in November 1685, and it never met again in his reign. In April 1688 he re-issued the Declaration of Indulgence and ordered the clergy to read it. Seven bishops who petitioned against it were tried for seditious libel and acquitted on 30 June, and the birth of his son James Francis Edward on 10 June raised the prospect of a Catholic dynasty.

Leading English figures invited William of Orange, James's nephew and son-in-law, who landed at Brixham on 5 November 1688. James's army deserted and he went into exile in France on 23 December. In February 1689 a Convention Parliament held that he had vacated the throne and installed William and Mary. James landed in Ireland in March 1689 with French help, but William defeated him at the Battle of the Boyne on 1 July 1690 (Old Style), and James fled to France, never to return. He lived at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, under Louis XIV's protection, until his death on 16 September 1701.

His son was recognised as James III and VIII by his supporters, later called Jacobites, and led a rising in 1715. Historians have disagreed on James: Macaulay cast him as a cruel absolutist, while some 20th-century writers praised his advocacy of religious tolerance, and more recent scholarship takes a middle course.
james-joyce: James Joyce was born on 2 February 1882 in Rathgar, Dublin, the eldest of ten surviving siblings. His father, John Stanislaus Joyce, was appointed rate collector by Dublin Corporation in 1887, but his unpredictable finances made family life chaotic. Joyce attended Clongowes Wood College and Belvedere College, and in 1898 enrolled at University College, Dublin, to study English, French and Italian, graduating in 1902. There he met the scholasticism of Thomas Aquinas, which influenced his thought for the rest of his life. He lapsed from the Catholic Church early, though his work is deeply influenced by Catholicism.

In October 1904 Joyce and Nora Barnacle went into self-imposed exile. He taught English in Pola and then Trieste, then part of Austria-Hungary, worked for eight months as a correspondence clerk in a Roman bank, and lived in Trieste until 1915, publishing Chamber Music and Dubliners there. He spent most of the First World War in Zurich, supported by a stipend that Pound and Yeats helped arrange and by regular sums from the editor Harriet Shaw Weaver, who supported him for the rest of his life.

In 1920 he moved to Paris, his main home for twenty years. Sylvia Beach, who ran the bookshop Shakespeare and Company, became one of his publishers. Ulysses was first published in Paris in 1922; its publication in the United Kingdom and the United States was prohibited as obscene, and copies were smuggled in and pirated until the mid-1930s, when publication became legal. He began Finnegans Wake in 1923, and suffered increasingly severe eye problems.

When Germany occupied France in 1940, Joyce moved back to Zurich. He underwent surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer on 11 January 1941 and died on 13 January, aged 58. Though he spent most of his adult life abroad, his fiction centres on Dublin. Ulysses is a model for fiction writers, and Finnegans Wake has become one of the key texts for French post-structuralism. His work and life are marked each year on 16 June, known as Bloomsday, in Dublin and in a growing number of other cities.
james-madison: James Madison Jr. was born on 16 March 1751 (5 March 1750 in the Old Style calendar) at the Belle Grove plantation near Port Conway in the Colony of Virginia. His father was a tobacco planter who, with an estimated 100 slaves and a 5,000-acre plantation, was among the largest landowners in Virginia's Piedmont. Madison joined the Patriots in 1774, believing that Parliament had overstepped its bounds in taxing the colonies,. With Thomas Jefferson he drafted the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, passed in 1786, which guaranteed freedom of religion and disestablished the Church of England.

Troubled in the 1780s by the weakness of the central government and the disunity of the states, Madison helped organise the Constitutional Convention, and his Virginia Plan was the basis of its deliberations. He became a leader of the movement to ratify the Constitution and wrote essays of The Federalist Papers with Alexander Hamilton and John Jay. Elected to the House of Representatives in 1789 after a hard contest against James Monroe, he introduced the Bill of Rights on 8 June 1789 after studying more than two hundred amendments proposed at the state ratifying conventions.

In the 1790s he opposed Hamilton's economic programme, including the First Bank of the United States, arguing that the Constitution gave Congress no power to create it, and with Jefferson he organised the Democratic–Republican Party. He served as Jefferson's Secretary of State from 1801 to 1809 and was elected president in 1808.

As president he tried to play Britain and France against each other over attacks on American shipping, and when this failed he led the country into the War of 1812. Madison was re-elected in 1812. The war ended inconclusively in 1815, but many Americans saw it as a second war of independence, and he presided over the creation of the Second Bank of the United States and the Tariff of 1816. During his presidency the United States acquired 26,000,000 acres from Native American tribes through treaties or war.

Madison retired to his plantation, Montpelier, in 1817,. Madison owned over one hundred slaves, and his views on slavery were conflicted throughout his life; his will freed none of them. He died of congestive heart failure at Montpelier on 28 June 1836, aged 85, and was one of the last prominent members of the Revolutionary generation to die. Historians regard him as one of the most significant of the Founding Fathers.
james-monroe: James Monroe was born on 28 April 1758 in Westmoreland County in the Colony of Virginia, the son of Andrew Spence Monroe, a craftsman who took part in protests against the Stamp Act, and Elizabeth Jones. In early 1776 he left college and joined the 3rd Virginia Regiment of the Continental Army as a lieutenant. At the Battle of Trenton he suffered a severed artery and nearly died; George Washington cited him for bravery and promoted him to captain. From 1780 to 1783 he studied law under Thomas Jefferson.

Monroe sat in the Congress of the Confederation from November 1783, where he helped to write the Northwest Ordinance. He opposed the ratification of the Constitution, and in 1790 was elected to the Senate. Washington appointed him minister to France in 1794 but recalled him in 1796. He was governor of Virginia from 1799 to 1802, and as Jefferson's envoy he helped to negotiate the Louisiana Purchase. He fell out with James Madison over the Monroe–Pinkney Treaty, but in April 1811 became Madison's Secretary of State, and in the War of 1812 also served as Secretary of War.

He defeated the Federalist Rufus King in 1816, and his inauguration on 4 March 1817 opened what was called the Era of Good Feelings, as the Federalists collapsed; in 1820 he was re-elected unopposed. He signed the Missouri Compromise, and in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819 the United States secured Florida and a border across the continent.

After his term ended in 1825 Monroe lived at Oak Hill in Aldie, Virginia, and was beset by financial difficulties. His wife Elizabeth died in 1830, and he moved to New York City, where he died on 4 July 1831. Monroe owned dozens of enslaved people, and sold property, including enslaved people, to pay debts. Polls of historians tend to rank him as an above-average president. He was a member of the American Colonization Society, and Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, is named after him. He was the last president to wear the powdered wig and knee-breeches of the late 18th century.
james-the-great: James was born into a family of Jewish fishermen on the Sea of Galilee. His parents were Zebedee and Salome, and Salome was a sister of Mary, the mother of Jesus, which made James a cousin of Jesus. He was the brother of John the Apostle. He is called the Greater to distinguish him from the other apostle James, the Lesser, the term meaning older or taller rather than more important. The Synoptic Gospels state that James and John were preparing to fish with their father by the shore when Jesus called them to follow him.

James, John and Peter formed an informal triumvirate among the Twelve. They were the only apostles present at three occasions of the ministry of Jesus: the raising of Jairus' daughter, the transfiguration and the agony in the Garden of Gethsemane. The brothers were nicknamed Boanerges, the Sons of Thunder. James and John, or in another tradition their mother, asked Jesus for seats on his right and left in his glory, and Jesus rebuked them.

The Acts of the Apostles records that Herod the king, usually identified with Herod Agrippa, had James executed by the sword. He was the first of the apostles to be martyred. The Armenian Apostolic Cathedral of St. James in the Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem is the traditional site, and his head is believed to lie under the altar of its Chapel of Saint James the Great.

The Historia Compostelana, commissioned by Diego Gelmírez in the 12th century, sets out the legend as it was believed at Compostela. James preached in Hispania as well as the Holy Land, and after his execution his followers carried his body by sea to Padrón in Galicia and overland to Santiago de Compostela. The Compostela tradition places the discovery of the relics in the 9th century, when Pelayo found them in the Libredon forest in the time of Bishop Theodemir and King Alfonso II. The pilgrimage route known as the Way of St. James began to form from that century.

A later tradition has him appear in battle for the Christian army at Clavijo, as Santiago Matamoros, and Spanish Christian armies took his name as a battle cry. The military Order of Santiago was founded in Spain in the 12th century. His emblem is the scallop shell, which pilgrims wore, and his feast day is 25 July.
james-vi-and-i: James was born on 19 June 1566, the only son of Mary, Queen of Scots, and Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, both great-grandchildren of Henry VII of England. He was entrusted to the Earl and Countess of Mar at Stirling Castle and crowned at the Church of the Holy Rude on 29 July 1567, at thirteen months, with John Knox preaching the sermon. Although his mother was a Catholic, he was raised as a Protestant. Four regents governed during his minority, which officially ended in 1578, though he did not fully control his government until 1583.

In Scotland James married Anne of Denmark in 1589, after sailing from Leith to fetch her when storms forced her ship to the coast of Norway. His visit to Denmark sparked an interest in witchcraft, and he attended the North Berwick witch trials. In 1597 and 1598 he wrote The True Law of Free Monarchies and Basilikon Doron, which set out the divine right of kings. He is credited with achieving most of his aims in Scotland.

Elizabeth I died early on 24 March 1603, and James was proclaimed king in London the same day. He tried to bring about a closer union of Scotland and England, but they stayed separate states with their own parliaments, judiciaries and laws, and from 20 October 1604 he styled himself King of Great Britain. He faced the Gunpowder Plot, discovered on the night of 4 to 5 November 1605, and quarrels with the English Parliament. After the plot he sanctioned harsh measures against English Catholics, including the Oath of Allegiance, though he was conciliatory to those who took it. He sponsored the translation of the Bible later named for him, and a 1604 revision of the Book of Common Prayer.

In his last years James suffered from arthritis, gout and kidney stones and was often seriously ill. He died on 27 March 1625. His reign in Scotland, of 57 years and 246 days, was the longest of any Scottish monarch. He was widely mourned, and his people had enjoyed peace and comparatively low taxation under him. He had often neglected government for the hunt, and his reliance on favourites at a scandal-ridden court weakened the image of monarchy that Elizabeth I had built. The courtier Anthony Weldon is credited with the epithet the wisest fool in Christendom.
james-watt: James Watt was born in Greenock, Renfrewshire, in January 1736, the eldest of the five surviving children of Agnes Muirhead and James Watt, a shipwright, ship owner and contractor who served as Greenock's chief baillie in 1751. The family's wealth came in part from his father's trading in slaves and slave-produced goods. His parents were Presbyterians and strong Covenanters, but he later became a deist. He was educated at home by his mother and then at Greenock Grammar School, where he showed an aptitude for mathematics while Latin and Greek failed to interest him. After leaving school he worked in his father's workshops, and when his father's ventures failed he left for Glasgow to find employment as a mathematical instrument maker.

In 1759 his friend John Robison called his attention to steam as a source of motive power. The Newcomen engine had been used for almost fifty years to pump water from mines and had hardly changed. Watt began to experiment, though he had never seen an operating steam engine, and came to realise the importance of latent heat, which his friend Joseph Black had discovered years before. His insight was that contemporary engines wasted energy by repeatedly cooling and reheating the cylinder, and he introduced the separate condenser to avoid this. Eventually he adapted the engine to produce rotary motion, which greatly broadened its use beyond pumping water.

Watt had great financial difficulties until he entered a partnership with Matthew Boulton in 1775. The first engines were installed in commercial enterprises in 1776, and for the next five years he installed more, mostly in Cornwall. Boulton and Watt charged an annual payment equal to one-third of the value of the coal saved compared with a Newcomen engine. Mine owners in Cornwall became convinced that his patent could not be enforced and withheld payments, and Watt had to go to court. The Soho Foundry formally opened in 1796, and in 1800 Watt retired, the year his fundamental patent and the partnership expired.

The story that Watt was inspired by a boiling kettle is probably apocryphal, possibly created by his son James Watt Jr.; Watt did not invent the steam engine but improved the existing Newcomen engine. He also devised a letter copying machine and studied chemistry, finding that a solution of chlorine could bleach textiles. In retirement he built machines for copying sculptures, which he never patented. He was a member of the Lunar Society of Birmingham. The chemist Humphry Davy said that those who considered him only a practical mechanic formed an erroneous idea of him, since he was equally distinguished as a natural philosopher and a chemist. He died on 25 August 1819, and the SI unit of power, the watt, is named after him.
jami: Nūr ad-Dīn 'Abd ar-Rahmān Jāmī was born on 7 November 1414 at Kharjerd in Khorasan to a Persian family. His father, Nizām al-Dīn Ahmad, had come from Dasht in the district of Isfahan, so his early pen name was Dashti; he later chose Jami for two reasons he gave in a poem, his birthplace of Jam and the Sufi Sheikh-ul-Islam Ahmad Jam. A few years after his birth the family moved to Herat, where he studied philosophy, mathematics, rhetoric, logic and Arabic and Persian literature at the Nizamiyya, with his father, also a Sufi, as his first teacher. He completed his studies at Samarkand and made a pilgrimage that raised his reputation across the Persian world.

In Herat Jami held an important position at the Timurid court and was a mentor and friend of the Turkic poet Alisher Navoi. He belonged to the Naqshbandi Sufi order and the school of Ibn Arabi, though he did not always follow it: on the dependence of God and creatures he wrote, "We and Thou are not separate from each other, but we need Thee, whereas Thou dost not need us." He became a Sufi shaykh in 1453 and defined terms such as sainthood and the levels of tawhid.

He wrote about eighty-seven books and letters. His major poetical work is the Haft Awrang (Seven Thrones), seven long masnavis, by his own admission influenced by Nizami, among them Salaman va Absal, an allegory of the stages of the Sufi path, and Yusuf and Zulaykha, based on the Quran. He also wrote the Kherad-name in the tradition of the Alexander Romance, three collections of lyric poems, the Nafahat al-Uns, a collection of biographies of Sufi saints, and the Baharestan, modelled on Saadi's Gulestan, for his surviving son Zia-ol-din Yusef. His commentary on the Arabic grammar Al-Kafiya was a staple of Ottoman madrasa curricula.

Jami was living in Herat at the end of his life. Dates for his death vary, but most sources give November 1492. The prince of Herat conducted his funeral, which large numbers attended. His poetry was popular across the Islamic East, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, and his works were used in schools from Samarqand to Istanbul and in the Mughal Empire. Babur, in the Baburnama, called him the foremost authority of the age in all of the sciences, and later Mughal emperors made versions of Yusuf and Zulaykha. Jami himself politely declined an invitation to settle in the Deccan.
jammu: Jammu lies on the Tawi river among low ridges in the Shivalik hills, with the Shivalik range to the north, east and southeast and the Trikuta Range to the northwest, at an average elevation of 300 metres. The old city overlooks the river from its north bank, and the newer neighbourhoods spread over the south bank. According to local tradition it was named after its founder Raja Jambulochan, who is believed to have ruled in the 9th century, and the tradition says the city is 3,000 years old, a claim historians do not support.

According to the Tarikh-i-Azmi, Jammu came into existence around 900 CE, and the state of Durgara, from which the names Duggar and Dogra come, is attested from about the same time. Its rulers are repeatedly mentioned in Kalhana's Rajatarangini. Timur's chronicles name Jammu, since he returned to Samarkand through it after invading Delhi in 1398. Babur's chronicles describe it as a powerful state of the Punjab hills ruled by Manhas Rajputs. Akbar brought the hill kingdoms under Mughal suzerainty, though their kings kept considerable autonomy, and the Mughal empire treated them as allies and partners.

After Mughal power declined in the 18th century the Jammu state under Raja Dhruv Dev of the Jamwal family asserted its supremacy among the Dugar states. Its height came under his successor Raja Ranjit Dev, who ruled from 1728 to 1780 and promoted religious freedom and security, which drew craftsmen and traders to settle there. Towards the end of his rule the Sikh misls gained ground; around 1770 the Bhangi misl forced Ranjit Dev to become a tributary, and his successor Brij Lal Dev was defeated by Mahan Singh of the Sukerchakia misl, who sacked Jammu.

In 1808 Ranjit Singh, son of Mahan Singh, annexed it to the Sikh Empire. In 1818 Kishore Singh, father of Gulab Singh, was appointed ruler of the Jammu principality, which began the Jamwal or Dogra dynasty that came to rule the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under British suzerainty.

Jammu is the winter capital of the union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, to which the offices move from Srinagar from November to April. It was the winter capital of the princely state from 1846 to 1952 and the capital of Jammu Province. The city is the cultural and economic centre of the Jammu division, and is about 600 kilometres from New Delhi.
jamshedpur: Jamshedpur lies at the confluence of the Swarnarekha and Kharkai rivers in the south of Jharkhand, bordered by Odisha and West Bengal, and is surrounded by the forested Dalma Hills. It is part of the larger Chota Nagpur Plateau, at an average elevation of 135 metres. The modern city was built over the village of Sakchi. Its central part includes old neighbourhoods such as Sakchi, Bistupur and Golmuri, while the south-east is largely industrial and residential. It is also known as Tatanagar.

At the end of the nineteenth century Jamshedji Tata met steelmakers in Pittsburgh to obtain the most advanced technology for his plant, and at the turn of the twentieth century he asked the geologist Charles Page Perin to find a site for India's first steel plant. The search for a place rich in iron, coal, limestone and water began in April 1904. His son Dorabji Tata chose the location at Sakchi, the project began in 1908 and the plant was operating by 1912. Lord Chelmsford named the city Jamshedpur in 1919, in honour of Jamshedji, whose birthday, 3 March, is marked as Founder's Day.

During the First World War Tata Steel supplied rail and steel to British military campaigns in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Salonica and East Africa. In the Second World War the city was a high-value target, and British and American troops and air bases were stationed in the region. On 1 January 1948 the Orissa Military Police opened fire on a crowd of over 50,000 at Kharsawan, who were protesting against its merger; official records state 35 deaths, while other sources give figures as high as 2,000. After independence the city lay in Bihar until it became part of the new state of Jharkhand on 15 November 2000.

The 2011 census counted 629,659 people in the city and 1,337,131 in the urban agglomeration. Hindi, Bengali, Santali, Bhojpuri, Odia, Urdu and Punjabi are the main languages. Tata Steel, in the centre of the city, occupies about a fifth of its area, and Tata Motors is the second major industry. The city is called India's first planned industrial city, envisioned by an Indian, planned by an American, named by a British Viceroy and landscaped by a German botanist. Jubilee Park, of 225 acres, is decorated with lights for about a week on Founder's Day.
jan-hus: Jan Hus was born at Husinec in southern Bohemia to peasant parents; the exact date is disputed and most of what is known of his early life is unsubstantiated. He took his name from the village, and the word hus means goose in Czech. He began teaching at the University of Prague in 1398, defended propositions of John Wycliffe in public for the first time in 1399, and was ordained as a Catholic priest in 1400. He became dean of the philosophy department in 1401 and a rector of the university a year later, and in 1402 he was appointed preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel.

Hus translated Wycliffe's Trialogus into Czech and helped distribute it, even though Church authorities banned many of Wycliffe's works in 1403. From his pulpit he denounced the moral failings of clergy, bishops and even the papacy. In 1409 King Wenceslaus IV, wishing the university to stay neutral in the Western Schism, decreed that the Czech nation should have three votes and the German nation only one. The German masters and students left for Heidelberg and Leipzig, more than a thousand of them by one estimate, and spread accusations of Bohemian heresy. Hus was excommunicated and spent two years in exile.

King Sigismund arranged a general council at Constance, which opened on 1 November 1414, and Hus agreed to attend under his promise of safe-conduct. At his trial on 8 June 1415 thirty-nine sentences drawn from his books were read to him. He declared himself willing to recant if his errors were proved from the Bible, but refused to confess that he had erred. He was burned at the stake on 6 July 1415, and his ashes were thrown into the Rhine.

On 2 September 1415 a hundred nobles of Bohemia and Moravia sealed a protest against his burning. Under Jan Žižka and later Prokop the Great the Hussites defeated crusades sent against them, and the fighting ended with the Basel Compacts of 1436, which allowed Bohemia to practise its own form of Christianity. A century later as much as ninety per cent of the Czech lands' inhabitants still followed Hussite teaching. In 1999 Pope John Paul II expressed deep regret for the cruel death inflicted on Hus. His followers survive in the Moravian Church.
jan-iii-sobieski: John Sobieski was born on 17 August 1629 at Olesko, now in Ukraine, into a noble family; his father, Jakub Sobieski, was Voivode of Ruthenia and Castellan of Kraków. He studied at Kraków and then spent more than two years travelling in western Europe with his brother Marek, learning French, German and Italian. Returning in 1648 to the Khmelnytsky Uprising, he fought at the siege of Zamość and at Berestechko. Sent to the Ottoman Empire as an envoy, he learned Turkish and Tatar and studied Ottoman tactics. In the Swedish invasion known as the Deluge he briefly swore allegiance to Charles X Gustav before returning to King John II Casimir in 1656.

Sobieski became Grand Hetman of the Crown in 1668. After defeating the Ottomans at the Battle of Khotyn on 11 November 1673, he was elected king on 19 May 1674 and crowned on 2 February 1676. He inherited a country devastated by almost half a century of war, with an almost empty treasury. The Treaty of Żurawno of 1676 brought a period of peace in which he reorganised the army into regiments and increased its artillery. His plans to conquer Prussia failed, and in 1683 he allied himself with Emperor Leopold I against the Ottomans, an agreement signed on 31 March.

On 12 September 1683 Sobieski, in joint command of Polish, Austrian and German troops, attacked the Ottoman army of Kara Mustafa at Vienna. The allies numbered about 65,000 to 76,000 men against about 143,000, and in the late afternoon he led the Polish hussars in a charge down the Kahlenberg that broke the Ottoman line. The Pope hailed him as saviour of Western Christendom. The war continued within the Holy League, and the Poles gained no lasting territorial rewards.

Sobieski died of a sudden heart attack at Wilanów on 17 June 1696, after increasing illness, and was succeeded by Augustus II the Strong. He is buried in Wawel Cathedral at Kraków, with his heart in the Church of the Transfiguration in Warsaw. He is remembered in Poland as a hero king, an image strengthened by nineteenth-century literature, although he failed to reform the Commonwealth or secure the throne for his heir. He was a patron of the astronomer Johannes Hevelius, and Wilanów Palace was the first of many palaces in the Commonwealth.
jan-palach: Jan Palach was born on 11 August 1948 and attended elementary school in Všetaty, where he was an avid reader of Jules Verne. His father died when he was 13, and he was raised in part by his grandfather. He graduated from a gymnasium in Mělník in 1966, attended the Prague School of Economics, and in September 1968 transferred to the Faculty of Arts at Charles University, where he studied history and political economics. In the summer of 1967 he worked on a chicken farm in the Soviet Union, where he instigated a strike with other Czech students that reduced their working day from ten hours to eight. On 7 November 1968 he took part in a demonstration for Czech independence.

On 16 January 1969, after the Warsaw Pact invasion that crushed the reforms of Alexander Dubček's government, Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square and suffered burns over 85 percent of his body. In a letter to several public figures he demanded the abolition of censorship and a halt to the distribution of Zprávy, the newspaper of the Soviet occupying forces, and called for a general strike. The burns specialist Jaroslava Moserová, who first treated him, said that he acted against the demoralisation of Czechoslovak citizens that the occupation had caused. He died in hospital three days later.

His funeral became a major protest against the occupation. On 25 February another student, Jan Zajíc, burned himself to death at the same place, and Evžen Plocek did so at Jihlava in April. Palach was first buried at the Olšany Cemetery in Prague. As the grave became a national shrine the secret police exhumed his remains on 25 October 1973 and cremated them; his ashes were returned to the Prague grave on 25 October 1990.

Between 15 and 21 January 1989, protests in Prague ostensibly in his memory but intended as anticommunist demonstrations grew into Palach Week, which the police suppressed. It is considered one of the demonstrations that preceded the fall of communism in Czechoslovakia ten months later. A bronze cross marks the spot outside the National Museum where he fell, and Jan Palach Square in Prague is named for him.
jan-van-eyck: Neither the date nor the place of Jan van Eyck's birth is documented; he was identified in the late sixteenth century as born in Maaseik, and his name is thought to derive from it. The first record of him comes from the court of John of Bavaria at The Hague, where between 1422 and 1424 payments were made to Meyster Jan den malre (Master Jan the painter), a court painter with the rank of valet de chambre who had one and then two assistants. He helped redecorate the Binnenhof palace.

After John's death in 1425 he became court artist and diplomat to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy. In 1428 he went to Lisbon to discuss a marriage contract between the duke and Isabella of Portugal, and on 18 October 1427 he attended a banquet in his honour at Tournai, where Robert Campin and Rogier van der Weyden were also present. A court salary freed him from commissioned work and gave him artistic freedom. He settled in Bruges, bought a house and around 1432 married Margaret, who was 15 years younger.

About 20 surviving paintings are confidently attributed to him, all dated between 1432 and 1439, and ten are signed with a variation of his motto ALS ICH KAN (As I Can), a pun on his name, which first appeared in 1433 on Portrait of a Man in a Turban. The Ghent Altarpiece, painted for Jodocus Vijdts and Elisabeth Borluut, was started before 1426 and completed by 1432. His high point is generally placed between 1434 and 1436, with the Madonna of Chancellor Rolin, the Lucca Madonna and the Virgin and Child with Canon van der Paele.

In portraits he used layers of thin translucent glazes that gave a rich depth of colour and vivid likenesses. He often signed and dated his frames, painting them to look like imitation stone, and many of his panels carry inscriptions in Greek, Latin or Dutch. Giorgio Vasari's claim that he invented oil painting is now considered an oversimplification.

Jan van Eyck died in Bruges on 9 July 1441 and was buried in the graveyard of the Church of St Donatian. Philip the Good made a one-off payment to his widow equal to the painter's annual salary. His unfinished works were completed by his workshop, which was run by his brother Lambert, who had the body moved into St Donatian's early in 1442. In 1454 Bartolomeo Facio named him the leading painter of his day, and his style was widely adopted by Rogier van der Weyden, Petrus Christus and Hans Memling.
jana-gana-mana: The song's lyrics first appeared in five stanzas in the Bengali magazine Tattwabodhini Patrika, the official publication of the Brahmo Samaj, of which Tagore was then editor, under the title Bharat Bhagya Bidhata. Tagore composed the melody himself in the raga Alhaiya Bilaval, possibly with some help from his musician grand-nephew Dinendranath Tagore.

It was first sung in public on the second day of the Indian National Congress session in Calcutta on 27 December 1911, by Tagore's niece in her school assembly. It was followed in January 1912 at the annual event of the Adi Brahmo Samaj, but remained largely unknown except to readers of the Brahmo journal. On 28 February 1919 Tagore sang it at the Besant Theosophical College in Madanapalle, where Margaret Cousins, the vice-principal, preserved it in Western notation from notes he provided, and where he made his own English translation, The Morning Song of India.

The poem is composed in Sadhu Bhasha, a heavily Sanskritised literary register of Bengali. Its five verses make up a hymn; only the first was adopted as the national anthem. A formal rendition takes about 52 seconds, and a shortened version of the first and last lines takes about 20 seconds.

Its first stanza names the provinces that were under direct British rule, among them Punjab, Sindh, Gujarat, Maratha, Dravida, Utkala and Bengal, but none of the princely states. Defenders hold that Tagore named only border regions in order to include all of India.

Subhas Chandra Bose chose the song as a national anthem while in Germany, and on 11 September 1942 the Hamburg Radio Symphony Orchestra played it as India's anthem at the founding meeting of the German-Indian Society. The Constituent Assembly closed its midnight session on 14 August 1947 with a unanimous performance, and adopted the first stanza as the National Anthem on 24 January 1950.

A dispute arose from reports in the British Indian press that a song of welcome to the Emperor had been sung at the 1911 Congress. Many historians hold the reports mistaken, because a different Hindi song, Badshah Humara, praised George V at the same session, and the nationalist press and the official Congress report distinguished the two. Tagore wrote in 1937 and 1939 that the Lord of Destiny of the song could never be George V or any other George. He had renounced a knighthood in 1919 in protest over the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
jane-austen: Jane Austen was born on 16 December 1775 in Steventon, Hampshire. Her father, George Austen, was the rector of the Anglican parishes of Steventon and Deane. He came from an old and wealthy family of wool merchants, but his own branch fell into poverty as each generation's eldest sons received the inheritances, and he was orphaned as a child. At sixteen he entered St John's College, Oxford, where he most likely met Cassandra Leigh, who came from the prominent Leigh family.

In 1809 her brother Edward offered his mother and sisters the use of a large cottage in Chawton, and Jane, Cassandra and their mother moved there on 7 July 1809. Life was quieter there than at any time since the family's move to Bath in 1800.

Austen wrote major novels before the age of 22 but was not published until she was 35. Like many women authors of her time she published anonymously. The ideal roles for a woman were then wife and mother, and a woman who wished to be a full-time writer was felt to be degrading her femininity. Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814) and Emma (1815) were moderate successes but did not bring her public fame in her lifetime.

Sir Walter Scott wrote an anonymous review of Emma in 1815, praising her realism. She died on 18 July 1817. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published after her death, and her brother Henry Austen's Biographical Note, dated December 1817, first identified her as the author of the novels. She left unfinished the novel Sanditon.

Austen's six novels implicitly interpret and criticise the English landed gentry at the end of the 18th century. Her plots often explore the dependence of women on marriage for social standing and economic security. Her works critique the sentimental novels of the second half of the 18th century and are part of the transition to 19th-century literary realism. Critics have praised her social commentary, wit and irony.

In 1832 Richard Bentley bought the remaining copyrights to her novels and in October 1833 released the first collected edition, in his Standard Novels series. Her novels have been continuously in print since. Her nephew published A Memoir of Jane Austen in 1869.
janissaries: The Janissary Corps was formed in the 14th century, either under Murad I or under his father Orhan. The Ottoman government took a tax of one-fifth on all slaves taken in war, and from this pool of men the sultans built a personal army loyal only to themselves. From the 1380s to 1648 the corps was filled through the devşirme, a levy of boys, predominantly Balkan Christians, who were enslaved, circumcised by force and converted to Islam. The levy was abolished in 1648. Jews were never subject to it.

A boy was first sent to a Turkish family in the provinces to learn Turkish and the customs of Ottoman society, and was then trained in the acemi oğlan, or cadet, school in the capital, where the brightest were selected for the palace institution of the Enderun. Janissaries lived in strict discipline in nearly monastic conditions and were forbidden to marry until retirement, typically in their forties. The devşirme was deeply resented among Christians in the Balkans, and in Serbian, Greek and Bulgarian memory it became one of the most enduring symbols of Ottoman rule.

Janissaries were kapıkulları, door servants of the sultan, neither freedmen nor ordinary slaves. They wore distinctive uniforms, lived in barracks, marched to the music of the mehter band and received regular salaries and pensions.
