Mountains surround it on three sides, and the highest point is Mount Huanggang in the Wuyi Mountains, at 2,157 metres. The Gan River flows through the whole province from south to north into Lake Poyang, the largest freshwater lake in China, which empties into the Yangtze. The Gan valley was historically the main north-south transport route of south China, one of the few easy corridors through the rugged south-eastern mountains. It carried trade between the North China Plain and the Yangtze valley and the territory of modern Guangdong, so the region was strategically important throughout much of Chinese history.

Jiangxi lay outside the sphere of early Chinese civilisation under the Shang, and peoples collectively known as the Baiyue probably lived there. Its north formed the western frontier of the state of Wu, and after Yue conquered Wu in 473 BCE, Chu took northern Jiangxi. Yuzhang Commandery, established at the start of the Han dynasty, was the first commandery set up there by a Chinese dynasty. It took its name from the original name of the Gan River, and Gan is now the province's abbreviation. In 291 it became its own zhou, Jiangzhou, under the Western Jin. In 733 the Tang divided the Jiangnan Circuit, and the western half, the Jiangnanxi Circuit, gave the province its modern name.

After the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, Jiangxi Province was established for the first time, and it took roughly its modern borders. After the fall of the Qing it became one of the earliest Communist bases. The Nanchang Uprising took place there on 1 August 1927. The government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was established at Ruijin in 1931, and in 1935, encircled by Nationalist forces, the Communists broke through and began the Long March to Yan'an. The brutal campaigns and purges of those years reduced the population by 40 per cent, to 13.8 million in 1936.

Nanchang is the provincial capital, and Ganzhou and Jiujiang are other major cities. Most of the population is Han Chinese, and the province is the centre of Gan Chinese, with some Hakka also spoken. It has deposits of copper, tungsten, gold, silver, uranium and lithium. After the opening of the Yuehan Railway in 1936 and of the Zhegan Railway in 1937, Jiujiang's port declined in importance. The province was fully under Communist control from the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
jihlava: Jihlava began as a Slavic market village on a trade route around 1200 and is first mentioned in 1233. Silver mining began in 1234, and the royal mining town was established between 1233 and 1240, making it the oldest mining town in what is now the Czech Republic. It was the first city in central Europe where mining law was codified. Miners came from Bavaria, Saxony and other German-speaking lands, and King Ottokar II's building regulations of 1270 set its rectangular plan around a large square.

By the end of the 14th century the richest deposits were exhausted and Jihlava turned to trade and cloth making. During the Hussite Wars it stayed a Catholic stronghold, and on 5 July 1436 a treaty was made there in which the Hussites acknowledged Sigismund as king of Bohemia. A fire in 1523 badly damaged the town, and Swedish troops captured it twice in the Thirty Years' War.

In the second half of the 18th century Jihlava was the second largest cloth producer in the Austrian Empire. In 1921 about 54 per cent of its people were German speakers, and it formed the centre of a German-speaking enclave. The synagogue was burnt in 1939, and most of the town's Jewish population, over 1,000 people, was deported and killed. After the Second World War most German speakers were expelled under the Beneš decrees.

Jihlava is the capital of the Vysočina Region, on the historic border of Moravia and Bohemia, about 110 kilometres south-east of Prague, with about 54,000 inhabitants. Its historic centre, a mixture of Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings, is protected as an urban monument reservation, and the early Gothic Church of Saint James the Great is a national cultural monument. Gustav Mahler lived there from 1860 to 1875, and his parents lie in the Jewish cemetery.
jilin: In ancient times the Jilin area was inhabited by the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and Wùjí, and the kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo ruled parts of it. The region then fell successively under the Xiongnu, the Xianbei state, Goguryeo, Balhae, the Khitan Liao dynasty, the Jurchen Jin dynasty and the Mongol Yuan dynasty. Under the Qing, much of the area was controlled by the General of Jilin, whose territory extended to much of what is now Russia's Primorsky Krai.

After Primorsky Krai was ceded to Russia in 1860, the government began to open the area to Han Chinese migrants, most of them from Shandong, and by the early 20th century the Han had become the dominant ethnic group of the region. In 1932 the area was incorporated into Manchukuo, a puppet state set up by Japan, with Changchun, then called Xinjing, as its capital. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the Red Army captured Jilin in Operation August Storm, and the region, with the rest of north-eastern China, passed to the Communists. Manchuria was the staging ground from which they conquered the rest of China in the Chinese Civil War.

In 1949 the province was smaller, taking in only the environs of Changchun and Jilin City, with its capital at Jilin City, while Changchun was an independent municipality. It was expanded to its present borders in the 1950s. During the Cultural Revolution it was enlarged again to include part of Inner Mongolia, giving it a border with Mongolia, but this was later reversed. The name comes from the Manchu phrase girin ula, meaning along the river, written in Chinese as jilin wula and shortened to Jilin.

Jilin is one of the three provinces of Northeast China, bordering North Korea and Russia to the east and south and Heilongjiang, Liaoning and Inner Mongolia. Its capital and largest city is Changchun, 113 kilometres west of Jilin City. The Changbai Mountains in the south-east hold its highest peak, Paektu Mountain at 2,744 metres, and the Yalu and Tumen rivers form parts of the border with North Korea. Agriculture centres on rice, wheat, maize and sorghum, and the province is known for ginseng and deer antlers used in Chinese medicine.
jilin-city: Jilin City lies in central Jilin Province, in a hilly area on the Songhua River, which surrounds much of the city and gives it the nickname River City. Four mountains stand round it: North Mountain (Beishan) to the west, Long Tan Mountain to the east, Zhuque Mountain to the north and Turtle Mountain to the south. With the river they form a bagua in the Taiji pattern. Beishan is the best known of them and is home to several Buddhist temples. The climate is humid continental, with long, cold winters. The Songhua is the only river in the region that does not freeze in winter, and water vapour rising from it crystallises on willow branches as rime ice in January and February.

Jilin City is one of the oldest cities in Northeast China. Under the Yongle Emperor, the Ming sought to extend control throughout Manchuria, and river fleets built here sailed several times to make local chieftains swear allegiance. After the Manchu-led Qing dynasty was established, the territory of today's Primorsky Krai was placed under Jilin's administration. As the Russian Empire advanced east towards the Pacific coast, the Qing government ordered a naval shipbuilding factory set up here in 1661.

Jilin was officially established as a fort city in 1673, when the Deputy Lieutenant-General Anzhuhu was ordered to build a castle. In 1676 the Military Governor of Ninguta was transferred to Jilin because of its more convenient location and growing military importance, and the city then developed rapidly. Its nickname comes from a line of a poem written by the Kangxi Emperor on his visit in 1682. Jilin remained important in the 18th and 19th centuries as one of the few cities beyond the Willow Palisade, with Qiqihar, Ninguta and Mukden.

When Manchukuo made Xinjing, now Changchun, its capital, Jilin's importance fell. By 1940 Jilin had 173,624 people and Xinjing 544,202. Soviet forces captured Jilin during the August Storm operation. It was the provincial capital of Jilin Province from the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 until Changchun took that role in 1956.

Jilin City is a prefecture-level city and the only major city in China that shares its name with its province. It co-hosted the Asian Winter Games in 2007, and winter sports such as skiing and skating are popular. Among its sights is Wulajie Old City, a walled Qing town downstream on the Songhua. It was a collecting point for local products sent to the imperial court, and the Kangxi Emperor went there in 1682 to fish for sturgeon. A Meteorite Museum there displays the largest stony meteorite of a documented meteorite fall.
jimena-diaz: Jimena, whose name is also spelled Ximena, was born before July 1046. She was the daughter of Diego Fernández, Count of Oviedo, himself the son of Count Fernando Flaínez, and of his wife Cristina, and she was a sister of Fernando Díaz, Count of Asturias. She married Rodrigo Díaz between July 1074 and 12 May 1076.

It is unclear whether she lived with her husband in the Taifa of Zaragoza during his first exile, from 1080 to 1086, when he led the army of its rulers, or whether she went to Asturias in those years. A legal action from Tol dated 1083 suggests that she kept a presence there even while the two were apart. At the start of his second exile, in 1089, she was imprisoned with her children Cristina, Diego and María by order of Alfonso VI. Nothing more is known of her until the end of 1094.

Rodrigo Díaz conquered Valencia on 17 June 1094 and secured it by his victory at the Battle of Cuarte on 21 October, after which Jimena rejoined him and stayed with him until his death. The principality he had founded was an independent state, and she succeeded him as its ruler. Their son Diego had been killed in 1097, fighting under Alfonso VI. A deed of gift that she made to the Cathedral of Valencia in 1101 survives with her signature. When the king judged the city impossible to defend, he escorted her back to Castile.

In 1103 she signed a document at the Monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña selling a monastery she owned to two canons of Burgos. This does not show that she spent her old age in the abbey, as the monastery maintained until the 18th century in the hagiographic texts known as the Legend of Cardeña; it is more likely that she lived her last years in or near Burgos. She died between 29 August 1113 and 1116, probably in 1116.

Through her daughters her descendants entered several ruling houses. Cristina married Ramiro Sánchez of Monzón and was the mother of King García Ramírez of Navarre, and María married first a prince of Aragon and then Ramon Berenguer III, Count of Barcelona. Jimena and her husband were buried at San Pedro de Cardeña. After the tombs were ransacked during the Napoleonic Wars the remains were reburied in Burgos, and they now lie in Burgos Cathedral.
jimmy-carter: James Earl Carter Jr. was born on 1 October 1924 in Plains, Georgia, at the Wise Sanitarium, where his mother worked as a registered nurse. He was the eldest child of Bessie Lillian Gordy and James Earl Carter Sr., a local businessman who ran a general store. The family settled in nearby Archery, a community populated almost entirely by impoverished Black families. His father was staunchly pro-segregation, yet allowed his son to befriend the children of the Black farmhands.

Carter graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1946 and joined the submarine service. In 1952 he began an association with the Navy's nuclear submarine program, led by Captain Hyman G. Rickover, who he later said had the most influence on his life after his parents. He then returned to Plains and expanded the family peanut-growing business.

Carter won a seat in the Georgia State Senate in 1962, after a repeat election because early counting was shown to be the result of fraudulent voting. He served from 1963 to 1967. Sworn in as the 76th governor of Georgia on 12 January 1971, he declared in his inaugural speech that the time for racial discrimination was over, which caused many segregationists who had supported him to feel betrayed. He merged about 300 state agencies into 22.

He announced his presidential campaign on 12 December 1974. Little known outside his home state, he was derided with the question Jimmy Who?. With the Watergate scandal fresh in voters' minds, his position as an outsider helped him, and he narrowly defeated the Republican incumbent Gerald Ford.

Inaugurated on 20 January 1977, Carter issued an unconditional amnesty for Vietnam War draft evaders. His administration negotiated the Camp David Accords, the Panama Canal Treaties and the second Strategic Arms Limitation Talks agreement, established diplomatic relations with China, and created the Departments of Energy and Education. His term was marked by inflation and recession, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran hostage crisis. He lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan in a landslide.

After the presidency Carter established the Carter Center to promote human rights, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002. He travelled widely to conduct peace negotiations, monitor elections and combat neglected tropical diseases, and he was a key figure in Habitat for Humanity. He died at his home in Plains on 29 December 2024, aged 100, and was buried next to his wife Rosalynn. Historians have generally rated his presidency below average, while his post-presidency, the longest in U.S. history, is viewed more favourably.
jin-song-wars: The two powers began as allies. After Wanyan Aguda united the Jurchen tribes and in 1115 named himself emperor of the Jin, the Song emperor Huizong sought his help against the Khitan-led Liao dynasty, hoping to recover the Sixteen Prefectures lost in 938. The Jin took the Liao capitals quickly, while Song attacks on Yanjing failed twice in 1122. By the treaty of 1123 the Song received only seven prefectures and agreed to pay the Jin 300,000 bolts of silk and 200,000 taels of silver a year.

The alliance soon broke down. Zhang Jue, a former Liao governor, turned his city over to the Song, though the treaty forbade harbouring defectors, and in 1124 Song officials asked for nine more prefectures. In November 1125 the Jin emperor Taizong ordered the attack.

Two Jin armies invaded. Kaifeng was first besieged on 31 January 1126, and after 33 days the new emperor Qinzong bought a withdrawal by ceding three prefectures; when he went back on the agreement the Jin returned and broke into the city on 9 January 1127. The Jin then tried to rule the north through puppet states, Da Chu in 1127 and Da Qi from 1130 to 1137. Gaozong, enthroned on 12 June 1127, was pursued as far as the sea in 1130, but the Song navy on the Yangtze and an insurgency in the north checked the invaders.

The peace of 1142 was broken twice. The Jin emperor Wanyan Liang invaded in 1161, was defeated at the Battle of Caishi in November and was assassinated by his own officers in December. Under the Song chancellor Han Tuozhou war was declared on 14 June 1206; the offensive failed, and the treaty of 2 November 1208 raised the tribute. Pressed by the Mongols, the Jin attacked the Song again from 1217 until a peace in 1224 ended the tribute. In 1233 the Song allied with the Mongols, and in 1234 their troops took Caizhou, where the Jin emperor Aizong killed himself.

Some two to three million Jurchens came to rule about 30 million Han Chinese in the north. Over half a million people fled south in 1126–1127. Lin'an, declared the capital in 1138, grew into a major commercial centre. The wars also spurred gunpowder weapons: the fire lance is first reported at the siege of De'an in 1132, and the iron-cased bombs the Jin used at Qizhou in 1221 are the first known hard-casing bombs. After the Jin fell the Mongols turned on the Song, which collapsed in 1279.
joachim-murat: Joachim Murat was born on 25 March 1767 at La Bastide-Fortunière in Guyenne, in the present-day department of Lot, the youngest of six surviving children. His father, Pierre Murat-Jordy, was an affluent yeoman, innkeeper and postmaster who also served as steward for the Talleyrand family. His parents intended him for the church, and he studied at the College of Saint-Michel at Cahors and then at the Lazarist seminary in Toulouse. In February 1787 he left the seminary, either expelled or, as others say, having run away with a girl, and enlisted in a cavalry regiment, the Chasseurs des Ardennes.

An ardent Republican, Murat served in the revolutionary army and, at the royalist rising of 13 Vendémiaire in October 1795, brought the cannons of the Camp des Sablons to the centre of Paris, which let General Napoleon Bonaparte save the National Convention. He went with Bonaparte to northern Italy in 1796, commanded the cavalry in Egypt, where he led the charge that broke the Ottoman line at Abukir on 25 July 1799, and played a pivotal role in the coup of 18 Brumaire. He married Caroline Bonaparte in a civil ceremony on 20 January 1800.
Napoleon made him a Marshal of the Empire on 18 May 1804 and Admiral of the Empire in 1805. He fought at Ulm, Austerlitz, Jena and Eylau, where he led a massed cavalry charge against the Russians.

Murat was Grand Duke of Berg and Duke of Cleves from 15 March 1806 and King of Naples from 1 August 1808. In the Russian campaign of 1812 he was the best cavalry commander of the Grande Armée at Smolensk and Borodino, though he showed little concern for the horses, which starved and tired on the long marches. After the Battle of Leipzig he reached a secret agreement with the Allies to save his throne.

When Napoleon returned from exile, Murat changed sides again, and on 15 March 1815 Naples declared war on Austria. His army of about 45,000 invaded the Papal States and Tuscany, but he was defeated at Occhiobello and decisively at Tolentino on 2 and 3 May, and returned to Naples on 18 May. After Waterloo he fled to Corsica and tried to invade Calabria with about 200 men. He was captured, sentenced to death and shot at Pizzo Calabro on 13 October 1815. Murat and Caroline had four children.
joan-of-arc: Joan was born c. 1412 in Domrémy, a small village in the Meuse valley. Her date of birth is unknown. Her parents were Jacques d'Arc and Isabelle Romée, and her father was a peasant farmer with about 20 hectares of land, who also collected taxes and headed the local watch. Joan was not taught to read and write and dictated her letters.

She grew up during the Hundred Years' War, in a France divided between Armagnacs and Burgundians since the Duke of Burgundy had the Duke of Orléans assassinated in 1407. Domrémy's people were loyal to the Armagnac cause. After a raid in 1425 in which cattle were stolen, Joan had her first vision. She later testified that she saw Saint Michael, and later Saint Margaret and Saint Catherine, and that she swore a vow of virginity to these voices.

Joan met Charles VII at Chinon in late February or early March 1429, when she was seventeen and he was twenty-six. Theologians at Poitiers declared her a good Catholic, and women directed by Yolande of Aragon verified her virginity. Charles commissioned plate armor for her, and she designed her own banner.

She reached Orléans on 29 April 1429. At first a figurehead for morale with no formal command, she gained the support of the Armagnac troops and sometimes advised their commanders. On 4 May her arrival rallied soldiers retreating from the bastille of Saint-Loup, and they took it. After the victory at Patay, Charles was crowned at Reims with Joan at his side. The sieges of Paris in September and La Charité in November failed, and her role in these defeats reduced the court's faith in her.

Burgundian troops captured Joan on 23 May 1430, and she was handed to the English in November. Her trial for heresy opened at Rouen on 9 January 1431 under Bishop Pierre Cauchon. She was accused of wearing men's clothes, of acting on demonic visions and of refusing to submit to the church. The trial was politically motivated: her claims, if unchallenged, would undermine the English claim to the French throne. She was burned at the stake on 30 May 1431.

A court reinvestigated the trial in 1456 and overturned the verdict, declaring it tainted by deceit and procedural errors. Joan became a national symbol of France after the French Revolution. She was canonized in 1920 and, two years later, declared one of the patron saints of France.
jodhpur: Jodhpur lies in the Thar Desert near the geographic centre of Rajasthan, about 250 kilometres from the border with Pakistan. Its name combines that of its founder, Rao Jodha, with the Sanskrit suffix pur, meaning city or settlement. The old city circles Mehrangarh Fort and is bounded by a wall with several gates. It is also called the Blue City for the dominant colour of the buildings in the old town. Average rainfall is around 362 millimetres but varies greatly: the famine year of 1899 brought only 24 millimetres and the flood year of 1917 as much as 1,178.

Marwar formed part of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire. A Rathore chieftain named Chunda received Mandore as a dowry from the Pratiharas and ruled there while the Tughlaq dynasty declined. Rao Jodha, a Rajput chief of the Rathore clan from Mandore, founded Jodhpur in 1459 after conquering the surrounding territory from the Delhi Sultanate. Mandore at first served as the capital but Jodhpur soon took over. The city stood on the road linking Delhi to Gujarat, which brought it a trade in opium, copper, silk, sandalwood and dates.

After Rao Chandrasen Rathore died in 1581, Akbar annexed the kingdom, and Marwar became a Mughal vassal with internal autonomy. Aurangzeb briefly took over the state around 1679 after the death of Maharaja Jaswant Singh, and Durgadas Rathore restored Jaswant's son Ajit Singh in 1707. Strife at court then invited the intervention of the Marathas. Under the British Raj Jodhpur was the largest state of Rajputana by area, and its Marwari merchants came to dominate trade across India. On 11 August 1947 Maharaja Hanwant Singh, the last ruler, signed the Instrument of Accession to India, having at first not wished to join. On 30 March 1949 the state became part of Rajasthan.

Jodhpur is the second-largest city of Rajasthan after Jaipur and the administrative headquarters of Jodhpur district and division, with about 1.6 million people. Its main sights are Mehrangarh Fort, Umaid Bhawan Palace, Jaswant Thada and the Ghanta Ghar clock tower, with Mandore Garden nearby. Local foods include Mirchi Bada and Mawa Kachori. It is a base for the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force, and a centre of the handicraft industry.
johann-gottfried-herder: Johann Gottfried Herder was born on 25 August 1744 in Mohrungen, now Morąg in Poland, in the Kingdom of Prussia, the son of a teacher. He grew up in a poor household and educated himself from his father's Bible and songbook. In 1762, at seventeen, he enrolled at the University of Königsberg, where he studied under Immanuel Kant and became a protégé of the philosopher Johann Georg Hamann, who disputed the claims of pure secular reason.

In 1764 Herder went to Riga as a Lutheran pastor and teacher, and there he wrote his first major works, which were literary criticism. In September 1770 he met the young Goethe at Strasbourg, whom his criticism inspired to develop his own style, which can be seen as the beginning of the Sturm und Drang movement. In 1771 he became head pastor and court preacher at Bückeburg. By the mid-1770s Goethe, by then a well-known author, used his influence at the court of Weimar to secure Herder the post of General Superintendent, and Herder moved there in 1776, where his outlook shifted towards classicism.

Late in his career he endorsed the French Revolution, which earned him the enmity of many colleagues, and he and Goethe experienced a personal split. He was ennobled in 1802, and he died in Weimar in 1803, aged 59.

Herder was one of the first to argue that language shapes the patterns by which each linguistic community thinks and feels. In his Treatise on the Origin of Language of 1772 he defined language as the natural organ of the understanding. His most ambitious work, the four-volume Ideas for a Philosophy of the History of Mankind, was published between 1784 and 1791 and is regarded as an origin of the modern school of historical thought.

Germans had no nation-state until the nineteenth century, and Herder was among the first German intellectuals to base a national consciousness mainly on language and literature. He taught that every nation carries its own standard of perfection, and that the true spirit of a people lies in its folk songs, poetry and dances. He collected folk songs, published in 1773 as Voices of the Peoples in Their Songs, which Achim von Arnim and Clemens von Brentano later drew on for The Boy's Magic Horn. He refused a rigid racial theory, writing that there is only one species of man throughout the whole earth.
johann-gottlieb-fichte: Fichte was born on 19 May 1762 in Rammenau and baptized a Lutheran, into a pious family that had lived in the region for generations. He was the son of a ribbon weaver, Christian Fichte, who married Maria Dorothea Schurich somewhat above his class. Fichte attended the foundation school at Pforta from October 1774. Miltitz's widow supported him until 1784, which let him study theology at Jena and Leipzig, but when she withdrew her help he had to leave without a degree and worked as a tutor for several families, and in Zürich met his future wife, Johanna Maria Rahn.

In the summer of 1790 Fichte began to study the works of Kant. After a disappointing interview with Kant at Königsberg on 4 July 1791 he wrote, in five weeks, the Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation. The first edition appeared without his name or preface and was believed to be a new work by Kant, until Kant cleared up the confusion and praised the author, and Fichte's reputation soared. He married Johanna on 22 October 1793. He was invited to the University of Jena and began lecturing in May 1794, expounding his system of transcendental idealism with success.

In 1798 he was accused of atheism over an essay in which he argued that the living moral order is itself God. He was dismissed in 1799 and, since every German state but Prussia had joined the outcry, went to Berlin, where he joined the circle of Friedrich and August Wilhelm Schlegel, Schleiermacher and Schelling. In 1807 and 1808 he delivered the Addresses to the German Nation, which attempted to define the German nation. In the new University of Berlin, founded in 1810, he was unanimously elected rector, but resigned in 1812 after friction. He died of typhus on 29 January 1814, aged 51.

Fichte rejected Kant's things in themselves, the supra-sensible reality beyond perception, as an invitation to skepticism. He argued instead that consciousness is not grounded in anything outside itself and that the phenomenal world arises from consciousness, the activity of the I, and moral awareness. In Foundations of Natural Right (1797) he argued that self-consciousness is a social phenomenon: an individual becomes aware of itself as free only when other rational subjects summon it, and mutual recognition is a condition for the individual I. He is also the originator of thesis, antithesis and synthesis, an idea often attributed to Hegel in error.
johann-heinrich-pestalozzi: Pestalozzi was born on 12 January 1746 in Zürich, the second of three children. His father, a surgeon and oculist, died when Pestalozzi was five, and the family was supported with the help of their maid, Barbara Schmid. On holidays he visited his grandfather, a clergyman in Höngg, where he learned of the poverty of country peasants.

He was educated to become a clergyman, but the failure of his first sermon and the influence of Rousseau led him towards law and politics. At 19 he joined the Helvetic Society, founded by his former teacher Johann Jakob Bodmer. He exposed cases of official corruption and was held under arrest for three days; this made him many political enemies and ended his hopes of a legal career. He then became a farmer, married Anna Schulthess in 1769 and built a house called Neuhof on heavily mortgaged land that proved unsuitable for farming.

He published the four volumes of Leonard and Gertrude between 1781 and 1787, drawing on his knowledge of peasant life. In it a mother, Gertrude, teaches her children to live morally, and a schoolteacher, a clergyman and a politician follow her example.

When serfdom was abolished in Switzerland in 1798 he decided to become an educator. After the French army invaded Stans in 1798, the Swiss government recruited him on 5 December to run a new orphanage there; the first orphans arrived on 14 January 1799, in a dreadful condition of body and mind. He then taught at Burgdorf from 1800 and opened the Educational Institute for the Children of the Middle Classes in its castle in October 1800.

The institute at Yverdon opened in July 1805 and attracted visitors and pupils from all over Europe, with governments sending educators to study there. Disunion grew among his colleagues, and a state commission in 1810 praised his ideas but not the institute's practices, ending hopes that Yverdon would become a state institution.

Pestalozzi returned to Neuhof and published his Swansong, which provoked bitter replies from Fellenberg and Niederer. He fell ill on 15 February 1827 and died in Brugg two days later. His methods were child-centred and based on individual differences, sense perception and the pupil's self-activity, and he held that human nature is essentially good. Friedrich Fröbel, the creator of the kindergarten, was his student, and Charles and Elizabeth Mayo founded the formal education of infant teachers in Britain after Charles lived with him at Yverdon from 1819 to 1822.
johann-sebastian-bach: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach on 21 March 1685 (Old Style; 31 March in the new), the eighth and youngest child of Johann Ambrosius Bach, a violinist and director of the town musicians, and Maria Elisabeth, née Lämmerhirt. The Bach family spanned four generations of musicians across Thuringia. Little is known of his early years, and his musical education is largely conjecture: he probably had early instruction from his father and sang with the local schoolboy choir. He studied theology, Latin and Greek at the Latin school, with poor attendance, perhaps because of a string of family deaths: his mother in May 1694 and his father in February 1695.

In 1703 Bach returned to Thuringia and worked as a musician for Protestant churches in Arnstadt and Mühlhausen. He also paid extended visits to the court at Weimar, where he expanded his organ repertory, and to the reformed court at Köthen, where he was mostly engaged with chamber music. By 1723 he was Thomaskantor in Leipzig, responsible for music in four Lutheran city churches and for the St. Thomas School. He decided to compose annual cycles of church cantatas, and wrote for the university's student ensemble, the Collegium Musicum.

Bach began publishing his organ and other keyboard music in 1726. His relations with his employer in Leipzig were difficult, as they had been in some earlier posts. They eased somewhat when Augustus III of Poland granted him the title of court composer of the Elector of Saxony in 1736. In his last decades he reworked and extended many earlier compositions. He died on 28 July 1750, aged 65, of complications following eye surgery. Four of his twenty children, Wilhelm Friedemann, Carl Philipp Emanuel, Johann Christoph Friedrich and Johann Christian, became composers.

Bach's music covers every genre of his time except opera: more than 200 sacred and secular cantatas, oratorios, Passions, motets and Latin church music, a large body of organ and keyboard music, and collections of orchestral and chamber music. He never left modern Germany apart from two brief trips to Bohemia, yet he knew European music widely. He sought to unite Italian and French traditions, particularly the Italian sonata and the French suite, in a mixed style. From about 1712 the music of Antonio Vivaldi was his most important influence.
johann-wolfgang-von-goethe: Goethe's grandfather, Friedrich Georg Goethe, moved to Frankfurt from Thuringia in 1687 and changed the spelling of the family name from Göthe. He worked first as a tailor and then opened a tavern. Goethe's father, Johann Caspar Goethe, had studied law in Leipzig and held the title of Imperial Councillor, but took no part in the official affairs of Frankfurt, then a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. He married Catharina Elisabeth Textor on 20 August 1748. Of their children only Johann Wolfgang and his sister Cornelia survived. The father had the boy taught by private tutors in Latin, Greek, French, Italian and English, as well as dancing, riding and fencing.

His tragedy Götz von Berlichingen (1773) first brought him recognition, and The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774) brought him enormous fame; it is arguably the world's first best-seller. Goethe settled in Weimar in 1775 and was ennobled by Karl August, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, in 1782. He sat on the Duke's privy council from 1776 to 1785, oversaw the reopening of silver mines at Ilmenau and carried out reforms at the University of Jena. After a tour of Italy in 1788 he published his first major scientific work, the Metamorphosis of Plants.

In 1791 he became managing director of the Weimar theatre. From 1794 he was friends with Friedrich Schiller, whose plays he premiered until Schiller's death in 1805. The first part of Faust appeared in 1808. His conversations and shared projects in the 1790s with Schiller, Herder, Fichte and others are collectively termed Weimar Classicism.

Goethe also studied natural science, writing on morphology and colour theory, and he told Johann Peter Eckermann he took more pride in his science of colours than in his poetry. By his death he had gathered 17,800 rock samples. He died in Weimar in 1832 of apparent heart failure. His last words are usually abridged to Mehr Licht!, 'more light', although the earliest account, by Karl Wilhelm Müller, gives a longer request to open a second shutter. Composers including Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt set his poems to music, and the mineral goethite is named after him.
johannes-brahms: Johannes Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833. His father, Johann Jakob Brahms, a double bass and horn player from Heide in Holstein, gave him his first musical training, and from 1840 he studied piano with Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel. The family lived in poor apartments in the Gängeviertel and struggled economically. By 1845 he had written a piano sonata in G minor, though his parents disapproved of his composing and thought a performer's career offered better prospects.

In 1850 Brahms met the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and accompanied him in recitals; this introduced him to the csardas, the foundation of the two sets of Hungarian Dances of 1869 and 1880. In 1853 he visited Joseph Joachim at Hanover, a lifelong friendship, and met Franz Liszt at Weimar. In autumn 1862 he first visited Vienna, and he based himself there increasingly and made it his home. In 1863 he became conductor of the Wiener Singakademie, programming Heinrich Schütz and J. S. Bach, and left in 1864 because the post took too much time from composing.

His First Symphony appeared in 1876, having been begun in the early 1860s; Hans von Bülow called it Beethoven's Tenth. The Second Symphony (1877), the Violin Concerto (1878) and the Academic Festival and Tragic Overtures (1880) followed. His admiration for Richard Mühlfeld, clarinettist of the Meiningen orchestra, revived his interest in composing after 1890 and led him to write the Clarinet Trio and Clarinet Quintet in 1891 and two Clarinet Sonatas in 1894.

His major works include four symphonies, two piano concertos and A German Requiem, which sets texts he chose from the Luther Bible and was composed over three periods of his life, with most of it written after his mother's death in 1865. He also wrote chamber music and hundreds of folk-song arrangements and Lieder. Cast as conservative absolute music against the New German School of Liszt and Wagner, his music was praised by Eduard Hanslick, and Hans von Bülow named him the heir of Bach and Beethoven, which Richard Wagner mocked. He died on 3 April 1897; the last notes he wrote were in the final chorale prelude of his Op. 122.
johannes-gutenberg: Johannes Gensfleisch zur Laden zum Gutenberg was born in Mainz, a wealthy city on the Rhine. His exact year of birth is unknown; a later document shows that he had come of age by 1420, and the year 1400 is commonly assigned to him for convenience. His father, Friele Gensfleisch zur Laden, was a patrician and merchant, and his mother, Else Wyrich, was the daughter of a shopkeeper and not of patrician lineage, so scholars assume he could never succeed his father at the mint. After conflict between patricians and guild craftsmen the family probably withdrew to Eltville in 1411 and again in 1413. A letter of March 1434 shows him living in Strasbourg, where he appears as a goldsmith.

In Strasbourg in 1440 Gutenberg is said to have perfected the secret of printing, but the record does not show what he was working on. In 1448 he was back in Mainz, borrowing from his brother-in-law. By 1450 a press was in operation, and he persuaded the moneylender Johann Fust to lend 800 guilders; Peter Schöffer, who became Fust's son-in-law, joined the enterprise. Work on the Bible began in 1452 with a second loan of 800 guilders, while the press also printed more lucrative texts such as Latin grammars and thousands of indulgences.

In 1455 he completed the 42-line Bible, of which about 180 copies were printed, three quarters on paper and the rest on vellum. Fust sued him in 1456 at the archbishop's court, claiming he had misused the funds, and the court gave Fust control of the Bible workshop. The Fust and Schöffer shop brought out the Mainz Psalter of August 1457, the first book with its printer's name and date.

Gutenberg seems to have kept or restarted a printing shop, and probably supplied the type for a Bible printed in Bamberg around 1459. On 18 January 1465 Archbishop Adolph von Nassau gave him the title of Hofmann, gentleman of the court, with a stipend and a court outfit. He died in 1468 and was probably buried in the Franciscan church at Mainz; the grave is lost. How he made his type remains unclear, and scholars still debate whether he used punches and matrices. After the sack of Mainz in 1462 printers went into exile, and Venice became the capital of printing, where Aldus Manutius published major Greek and Latin texts.
johannes-kepler: Johannes Kepler was born on 27 December 1571 in the Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt. His parents were Lutheran, but he is presumed to have been baptised a Catholic, since Protestant baptisms were not permitted there. His grandfather had been Lord Mayor, but the family fortune was in decline. His father, a mercenary, left when Johannes was five, and his mother, Katharina Guldenmann, was a healer and herbalist. Born prematurely, Kepler said he had been a weak and sickly child, yet he impressed travellers at his grandfather's inn with his mathematical ability.

Kepler taught mathematics at a seminary school in Graz from 1594 to 1600. In 1600 he went to Prague, where Tycho Brahe secured him a place on the project of the Rudolphine Tables. Two days after Tycho's death on 24 October 1601, Kepler was appointed his successor as imperial mathematician to Emperor Rudolf II, and he regarded the next eleven years as the most productive of his life. His main duty was to give astrological advice to the emperor, although he took a dim view of attempts to predict specific events.

In 1612 he moved to Linz as District Mathematician and teacher, keeping his court post. The Rudolphine Tables were completed in 1623 but, because of the emperor's publishing requirements and negotiations with Tycho's heir, printing at Ulm was finished only in September 1627. He then presented them to the emperor in Prague. He died on 15 November 1630.

His first major work, Mysterium Cosmographicum of 1596, nested the five Platonic solids between the spheres of the six known planets. In Astronomia nova of 1609 he replaced the notion of a planetary orb, a spherical shell carrying the planet, with that of an orbit resulting from physical causes, and he set out the first two laws of planetary motion by analysing the orbit of Mars from Tycho's observations. The Epitome Astronomiae Copernicanae contained all three laws. Harmonice Mundi of 1619 explained the proportions of the natural world in terms of music.

In Astronomiae Pars Optica of 1604 he described the inverse-square law of light's intensity, and he is generally considered the first to recognise that the eye's lens projects an inverted image on the retina. He supported Galileo Galilei's discovery of the moons of Jupiter. His laws were not at once accepted: Galileo and René Descartes ignored the Astronomia nova.
johannes-vermeer: Vermeer was baptized in the Reformed Church on 31 October 1632. His mother, Digna Baltens, came from Antwerp. His father, Reijnier Janszoon, was a silk weaver from Antwerp who moved to Delft, began dealing in paintings and joined the Guild of Saint Luke as an art dealer in 1631. In 1641 he bought a larger inn on the market square. When Reijnier died in October 1652, Vermeer took over the family art business. In April 1653 he married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic. Her mother, Maria Thins, was at first opposed, and it was probably she who insisted that he convert to Catholicism. The couple lived in her house on the Oude Langendijk for the rest of his life, and Catharina gave birth to 15 children.

It is unclear where Vermeer trained. Some have proposed Carel Fabritius, but there is no hard evidence, and others suggest Abraham Bloemaert. He became a member of the Guild of Saint Luke on 29 December 1653 and was elected its head in 1662, then again in 1663, 1670 and 1671, which shows that his colleagues regarded him as an established craftsman. He worked slowly, probably producing about three paintings a year, and he also dealt in art. His patrons for much of his career were Pieter van Ruijven and his wife Maria de Knuijt, who bought much of his output. That kept him afloat but limited the spread of his fame.

Vermeer used the expensive pigment ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli, more lavishly and earlier than any other artist of the century, often as an underpaint beneath earth colours. He worked in domestic interiors, usually lit from the left, and the same rooms, furniture and women appear in many of his pictures. In 1672, the Rampjaar, French troops under Louis XIV and forces from Münster and Cologne invaded the Dutch Republic. The art market collapsed, and a painting sold that year was Vermeer's last sale.

Vermeer died on 15 December 1675, aged 43, after a short illness, and was buried the same day in the Old Church. His widow told her creditors that the burden of his debts and unsold stock had brought on his death. She had children to raise and asked the High Court for relief from debt, and the microscopist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was named trustee of the estate.

Vermeer was little known outside Delft. After his death he fell into obscurity, was barely mentioned in Arnold Houbraken's survey of 1718 and was omitted from later surveys for nearly two centuries. In the 19th century Gustav Friedrich Waagen and Théophile Thoré-Bürger rediscovered him. Thoré-Bürger called him the Sphinx of Delft, because so little was known of his life, and attributed 66 works to him, of which 34 are universally accepted today.
johannesburg: Johannesburg lies on the Highveld, the eastern plateau of South Africa, at an elevation of 1,753 metres. The former central business district sits on the southern side of the Witwatersrand ridge, which marks the watershed between the Limpopo and Vaal rivers. The climate is subtropical highland, with hot summers and afternoon thundershowers from October to April and dry, sunny winters with cold nights. The city is mineral-rich, and the Witwatersrand has long been at the centre of the international gold trade.

San hunter-gatherers who used stone tools lived in the area up to ten centuries ago. By the mid-18th century the wider region was largely settled by Sotho–Tswana communities, whose stone-walled towns and villages left ruins across the former Transvaal. The main Witwatersrand gold reef was discovered in June 1884 on the farm Vogelstruisfontein, which set off the Witwatersrand Gold Rush and the founding of Johannesburg in 1886. The origin of the name is disputed, and records of the choice were lost. Within ten years the city had 100,000 people.

Like many late 19th-century mining towns it was rough and disorganised. White miners came from all continents, African men were recruited to do unskilled mine work, and the Zulu men known as the AmaWasha dominated laundry work. As the value of controlling the land rose, tensions grew between the Boer-dominated Transvaal government in Pretoria and the British, which led to the Jameson Raid, ending in fiasco at Doornkop in January 1896. In the Second Boer War (1899–1902) British forces under Field Marshal Frederick Sleigh Roberts occupied the city on 30 May 1900.

In 1917 it became the headquarters of the Anglo-American Corporation, founded by Ernest Oppenheimer. In the 1950s and early 1960s the apartheid government built the massive agglomeration of townships known as Soweto, which was designated a blacks-only city until 1994 and became the centre of the 1976 Soweto Uprising. After apartheid ended, the old city and the surrounding townships and settlements were unified administratively in the City of Johannesburg Metropolitan Municipality.

Johannesburg is the capital of the province of Gauteng, the largest city in South Africa and its economic capital. It is the seat of the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, and home to the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the largest on the continent. It has two major public universities, the University of the Witwatersrand and the University of Johannesburg. Its spatial inheritance from apartheid is still visible in the layout of its suburbs and townships.
john-adams: John Adams was born on 30 October 1735 on the family farm in Braintree, Massachusetts, the son of John Adams Sr., a farmer, cordwainer, deacon and militia lieutenant, and Susanna Boylston Adams. He entered Harvard College at sixteen and graduated in 1755. His father expected him to become a minister, but he taught school briefly, chose the law and was admitted to the bar in 1759. He joined the colonial cause after hearing James Otis Jr.'s 1761 challenge to the writs of assistance, and he rose to prominence in opposing the Stamp Act, writing the Braintree Instructions of 1765.

After British soldiers killed five civilians in the Boston Massacre of 5 March 1770, Adams defended them when no other attorney would, holding that everyone has the right to counsel and a fair trial. A delegate to the First Continental Congress in 1774, he seconded the Lee Resolution on 7 June 1776 and, as one of the Committee of Five, helped Jefferson with the Declaration of Independence. As a diplomat he worked on the Model Treaty with France, secured a Dutch loan, helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris and in 1785 became the first American ambassador to Great Britain. He was the primary author of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 and served as vice president from 1789 to 1797.

As president he kept the country out of the war between Britain and France. French seizures of American ships led to the undeclared Quasi-War, during which Congress created the Navy Department. In June 1798 he signed the Alien and Sedition Acts at the urging of his wife and cabinet, though he had not promoted them. He appointed John Marshall Chief Justice and signed the law establishing the Library of Congress.

Defeated by Jefferson in 1800, Adams retired to Peacefield in Quincy. After years of silence the two men resumed their friendship through a continuing correspondence. He lived to see his son John Quincy Adams become president in 1825 and died at Peacefield on 4 July 1826. His pamphlet Thoughts on Government of 1776 was long influential. He was accused of monarchist sympathies, which he denied, and he never owned a slave. Benjamin Franklin said of him that he was always an honest man, often a wise one, but sometimes absolutely out of his senses.
john-amos-comenius: Comenius was born on 28 March 1592 in the Margraviate of Moravia. His exact birthplace is uncertain: Uherský Brod, Nivnice and Komňa are all possibilities. He was the youngest child and only son of Martin Komenský and Anna Chmelová, who belonged to the Bohemian Brethren. His parents and two of his sisters died in 1604. Poverty delayed his formal schooling until his later teens. He studied at the Herborn Academy and the University of Heidelberg, and in 1616 was ordained in the ministry of the Brethren.

In 1620 Comenius became pastor and rector at Fulnek. Religious wars cost him his property and writings in 1621, and in 1627 he led the Brethren into exile when the Habsburg Counter-Reformation persecuted Protestants in Bohemia. He settled at Leszno in Poland, where he headed the gymnasium. His Janua linguarum reserata, or The Gate of Languages Unlocked, brought him wide fame. In 1638 the Swedish government asked him to draw up a scheme for its schools, and in 1641 he joined a commission of the English Long Parliament on educational reform, which the English Civil War interrupted.

He later worked in Sweden, Elbląg, England and, from 1650, Sárospatak in Hungary, where he taught until 1654. During the Deluge in 1655 he declared for the Protestant Swedish side, and in 1656 Polish Catholic partisans burned his house, manuscripts and printing press, destroying the manuscript of Pansophia. He took refuge in Amsterdam, where he died in 1670 and was buried in Naarden.

Comenius wrote more than forty educational titles. They rested on shared ideas: learning foreign languages through the mother tongue, gaining ideas through objects rather than words, beginning with what is familiar to the child, making learning a pleasure and making instruction universal. His Didactica Magna outlined a system of schools from kindergarten to university. The Orbis Pictus of 1658 was among the most widely circulated school books for the next century and the first successful use of illustrations in teaching youth.

He also led the seventeenth-century pansophic movement, which sought to organise all human knowledge. As a bishop of the Unity of the Brethren he wrote the Labyrinth of the World and Paradise of the Heart. His influence was little recognised for much of the eighteenth century, but it has been acknowledged since the middle of the nineteenth. Czechs idealised him as a symbol of their nation during the National Revival, and 28 March is Teachers' Day in the Czech Republic.
john-cabot: Cabot was born in Italy, the son of Giulio Caboto; Gaeta and Castiglione Chiavarese have both been proposed as his birthplace. He became a citizen of the Republic of Venice in 1476, and by 1484 he was married to Mattea, with sons Ludovico, Sebastian and Sancto. He fell into debt and left Venice as an insolvent debtor by 5 November 1488. In Valencia his harbour proposals were rejected, and in Seville a bridge contract ended when the project was abandoned on 24 December 1494. He probably reached England in mid-1495.

On 5 March 1496 Henry VII gave Cabot and his three sons letters patent to sail to unknown lands. The patent required expeditions to leave from Bristol, with the king taking one fifth of the profit. A first attempt, probably in the summer of 1496, was abandoned because of a confused crew, short supplies and bad weather.

In 1497 Cabot sailed in the Matthew, a small ship of about 50 tons with a crew of 18 to 20. A Bristol chronicle gives her departure as 2 May and return as 6 August, with the land found on 24 June. The sources disagree on details. Cabot is said to have landed once, raised the Venetian and papal banners, and met no one. Newfoundland, Cape Breton Island, Labrador and Maine have all been proposed for the landfall. The king rewarded him with £10 and then a pension of £20 a year.

In 1498 Cabot left Bristol with a fleet reported as five ships, some carrying goods for trade. A storm forced one into Ireland, and the Spanish envoy said the others went on. It is not known whether he died at sea, died after returning, or stayed in the Americas. The historian Alwyn Ruddock argued that he returned in 1500, and researchers of the Cabot Project at the University of Bristol have sought evidence for this. Cabot Tower in Bristol and another in St John's, Newfoundland, both begun in 1897, commemorate his voyage.
john-calvin: John Calvin was born Jehan Cauvin on 10 July 1509 at Noyon, in Picardy, where his father Gérard was the cathedral notary and intended his sons for the priesthood. He was educated in Paris, trained as a humanist lawyer and published a commentary on Seneca's De Clementia in 1532. He broke from the Roman Catholic Church around 1530. After violence against Protestants in France he fled to Basel, where in March 1536 he published the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion.

William Farel recruited him for the Reformation in Geneva, but the city council resisted their proposals and both men were expelled. At Martin Bucer's invitation Calvin became minister of a French refugee church in Strasbourg. Invited back to Geneva in 1541, he saw the council pass the Ecclesiastical Ordinances on 20 November 1541, which defined four orders of ministry and created the Consistory, a court of elders and ministers with no civil jurisdiction. Opposition came from wealthy, interrelated families he called libertines, led by Ami Perrin from about 1546.

Michael Servetus, a Spanish physician whose book rejected the Trinity, arrived in Geneva on 13 August 1553 and was burned at the stake for heresy by the city council after Calvin denounced him. Sebastian Castellio broke with Calvin over the treatment of heretics. In January 1555 the council confirmed that the Consistory should regain its powers, and Calvin's authority was practically uncontested in his last years. The final edition of the Institutes appeared in 1559, in four books and eighty chapters. His theology included predestination and God's absolute sovereignty in salvation, and his critics such as Jérôme-Hermès Bolsec attacked the first.

Calvin preached his last sermon on 6 February 1564 and died on 27 May 1564, aged 54. He was buried in an unmarked grave in the Cimetière des Rois. Geneva sheltered English exiles from 1555, among them John Knox, who carried his ideas to Scotland and England. His reforms reached the Netherlands and the Palatinate, where the Heidelberg Catechism was written in 1563.
john-f-kennedy: John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born on 29 May 1917 in Brookline, Massachusetts, to Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., a businessman and politician, and Rose Kennedy. His maternal grandfather and namesake, John F. Fitzgerald, was a U.S. congressman and two-term mayor of Boston. He graduated from Harvard University in 1940. Medically disqualified from the Army's Officer Candidate School because of chronic back problems, he joined the United States Naval Reserve on 24 September 1941.

With his father's backing, Kennedy won the Democratic primary for Massachusetts's 11th congressional district in 1946 and sat in the House of Representatives from 1947 to 1953. In 1952 he narrowly defeated Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. for the Senate. After several spinal operations he published Profiles in Courage, which won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography in 1957.

He announced his candidacy for the presidency on 2 January 1960, took the nomination on the first ballot at the Democratic convention in Los Angeles, and chose Lyndon Johnson as his running mate. He was sworn in on 20 January 1961.

Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas at 12:30 p.m. on 22 November 1963, shot as his motorcade passed through Dealey Plaza, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Hospital at 1:00 p.m., aged 46. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested and, on 24 November, shot dead by Jack Ruby before he could be prosecuted. The Warren Commission concluded that Oswald had acted alone, though conspiracy theories persist. Many of Kennedy's proposals passed after his death, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
john-glenn: John Herschel Glenn Jr. was born on 18 July 1921 in Cambridge, Ohio, and grew up in New Concord, where his father ran a plumbing business. He first flew in an airplane with his father at the age of eight and built model airplanes. When the United States entered the Second World War he left college and became a Navy aviation cadet in March 1942, then transferred to the Marine Corps and was commissioned a second lieutenant in 1943. He married Anna Margaret (Annie) Castor on 6 April 1943. In the Korean War he flew 63 combat missions, and he later attended the Naval Test Pilot School. In 1957 he made the first supersonic transcontinental flight across the United States.

NASA was established on 1 October 1958 after the launch of Sputnik 1, and Project Mercury aimed to put a man into Earth orbit. Glenn was one of the Mercury Seven military test pilots selected in 1959 as the first American astronauts, and he was backup pilot for the first two crewed Mercury flights. For Mercury-Atlas 6 he named his spacecraft Friendship 7. On 20 February 1962 he became the first American to orbit the Earth, circling it three times, and the third American and fifth person in space. Buzz Aldrin wrote that the flight helped to galvanize the country's will to meet the technical challenges of human spaceflight.

Glenn resigned from NASA on 16 January 1964 and announced his candidacy for the Senate from Ohio, becoming the first astronaut-politician. He was elected to the Senate in 1974 and served until January 1999. He was chief author of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Act of 1978. In 1998, at the age of 77, he flew on the Space Shuttle Discovery on mission STS-95, as the oldest person then to enter Earth orbit.

Glenn received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor in 1978, entered the US Astronaut Hall of Fame in 1990 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. He and Annie were married for 73 years, and they had two children. He died on 8 December 2016, aged 95, the oldest and last surviving of the Mercury Seven.
john-ii-of-france: John was born on 26 April 1319 and was nine years old when his father, Philip VI, was crowned. Philip's accession was unexpected, since all three sons of Philip IV had died without sons and Edward III of England had been passed over. John became Duke of Normandy in 1332, where much of the nobility was already allied with the English. The defeat at Crécy on 26 August 1346 and the fall of Calais in 1347 damaged royal prestige. His first wife, Bonne of Bohemia, died of the Black Death on 11 September 1349, and on 9 February 1350 he married Joan I, Countess of Auvergne.

Philip VI died on 22 August 1350, and John was crowned at Reims on 26 September. In 1351 he issued military ordinances to address disorganisation, discipline and pay in the army, and on 16 November founded the Order of the Star, a chivalric order meant to unify the nobility under royal leadership and to counter Edward III's Order of the Garter. His favourite Charles de la Cerda, the Constable of France, was stabbed to death in 1354 by several barons. John signed the Treaty of Mantes with Charles II of Navarre on 22 February 1354, but the peace did not last.

In July 1356 Edward, the Black Prince, led a great chevauchée through France, and the two armies met southeast of Poitiers. John was captured and held in England, including at the Savoy Palace and the Tower of London, with royal privileges. The Treaty of Brétigny, drafted in May 1360, set his ransom at 3 million crowns, about two or three years of the Crown's revenue. John left the Tower on 30 June 1360. His son Charles, as regent, had overcome several rebellions, and John created the franc to stabilise the currency.

In 1363 John's son Louis, a hostage in exchange for him, broke his parole and escaped from Calais. John resolved to return to captivity, replying that if good faith were banned from the earth, it should find asylum in the hearts of kings. He landed in England in January 1364 and fell ill with an unknown malady. He died at the Savoy Palace in April 1364 and was buried at the Basilica of Saint Denis. He created seven duchies and counties, more than any other French monarch.
john-king-of-england: John was the youngest son of King Henry II of England and Eleanor, Duchess of Aquitaine. He was born around Christmastide in 1166 or 1167, and historians debate the precise date. His father's lands, Anjou, Normandy and England, with Eleanor's Aquitaine, formed the Angevin Empire, a fragile union whose parts had their own traditions and governments. As a younger son John was not expected to inherit significant lands, and his father jokingly called him Lackland. In 1177 Henry appointed him Lord of Ireland. When Richard became king in 1189 he made John Count of Mortain and married him to the wealthy Isabella of Gloucester.

After Richard died on 6 April 1199, John's claim rivalled that of Arthur of Brittany, son of John's elder brother Geoffrey. John had the support of most English and Norman nobles and was crowned at Westminster Abbey, while Philip II of France backed Arthur. The peace treaty of Le Goulet in 1200 recognised John's continental lands. War returned after he married Isabella of Angoulême in August 1200, having set aside his first wife. Shortages of resources and his treatment of Norman, Breton and Anjou nobles led to the collapse of his empire in northern France in 1204. He spent the next decade trying to regain it, raising large revenues and reforming his forces. His judicial reforms had a lasting effect on English common law.

A dispute with Pope Innocent III over the election of Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury led Innocent to ban church services in England from 1208 until 1214 and to excommunicate John from 1209 until 1213. In 1209 John invaded Scotland and forced William the Lion to sign the Treaty of Norham, with a payment of £10,000.

In 1214 John's final campaign to retake Normandy failed when the French defeated his allies at the Battle of Bouvines. Barons who were unhappy with his fiscal policies and his treatment of nobles rebelled, many of them northerners who owed him large sums. John and the barons agreed to Magna Carta in 1215 as a peace treaty, but neither side complied with it, and civil war began. He died on 19 October 1216. Contemporary chroniclers mostly criticised him. Jim Bradbury describes the present view as that of a hard-working administrator, an able man and an able general, while historians also point to faults such as pettiness, spitefulness and cruelty.
john-knox: Knox was born in or near Haddington, East Lothian, sometime between 1505 and 1515, the son of a merchant. He studied at the University of St Andrews or possibly Glasgow, under John Major, and was ordained a Catholic priest in Edinburgh on Easter Eve 1536. He appears in the records as a priest and notary in 1540 and became tutor to the sons of two lairds who had embraced the new religious ideas. After the murder of Cardinal David Beaton in 1546 he became chaplain to the garrison of St Andrews castle. French galleys besieged it, and on 31 July 1547 the garrison surrendered; Knox was taken to France and forced to row in the galleys until 1549.

Knox took refuge in England and on 7 April 1549 was licensed to work in the Church of England. He became a royal chaplain to Edward VI and influenced the wording of the Book of Common Prayer. When Mary I restored Catholicism he left England for Frankfurt and then Geneva, where he met John Calvin. He was elected minister of the English congregation there and arrived on 13 September 1556.

Back in Scotland in 1559, Knox preached a sermon at Perth on 11 May after which a mob gutted the church and attacked two friaries. In August 1560 the Scottish Parliament asked him and five other ministers named John to draw up a confession of faith. The Scots Confession was presented within four days and approved, and Parliament abolished papal jurisdiction and forbade the Mass. The Book of Discipline of January 1561 was not approved, mainly for reasons of finance.

After Mary, Queen of Scots, arrived in August 1561 and heard Mass at Holyrood, Knox protested from the pulpit of St Giles' and refused to moderate his preaching when she summoned him. In 1564 he married Margaret Stewart, aged seventeen, when he was a widower of fifty. His influence waned as the nobility supported Mary. He died on 24 November 1572. His will declared that he had corrupted and defrauded none, and the small sum he left showed that he had not profited from the Kirk. He wrote his History of the Reformation in Scotland between 1559 and 1566.
john-locke: John Locke was born on 29 August 1632 in the village of Wrington, Somerset, to Puritan parents. His father, also John Locke, was an attorney who served as clerk to the Justices of the Peace in Chew Magna, one of whom was Alexander Popham, a Member of Parliament for Bath. Locke was 10 when the English Civil War began, and his father fought for the Parliamentarian side as a captain of cavalry under Popham.

In 1647, under Popham's sponsorship, he became a student at Westminster School in London. Locke wrote of those years, "I found myself in a storm." He then won a place at Christ Church, Oxford, where he spent 15 years, first as a student and then as a tutor, pursuing medical and other scientific interests.

In 1665 Locke travelled outside England for the first time, as secretary to Sir Walter Vane on a failed diplomatic mission to the Elector of Brandenburg. In 1666 he met Anthony Ashley Cooper, later Lord Shaftesbury, and in 1667 moved into Shaftesbury's London home as his personal physician. He studied medicine there under Thomas Sydenham, and was probably instrumental in persuading Shaftesbury to undergo the surgery that saved his life. Locke was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1668.

After Shaftesbury fell from royal favour and died, Locke spent five years in political exile in the Netherlands (1683–85), where he wrote some of his most important works. He returned to England in 1689, served as a Commissioner of Trade and Plantations and retired because of ill health. He is also listed as a shareholder in the Royal Company of Adventures Trading to Africa, which traded in slaves from 1663. He died on 28 October 1704.

In his Letters Concerning Toleration (1689–1692) Locke argued that earthly judges cannot dependably evaluate competing religious truth-claims, that belief cannot be compelled by violence, and that enforcing uniformity would cause more disorder than allowing diversity. In the Essay Concerning Human Understanding he held that the mind is at birth a blank slate, tabula rasa, and that knowledge comes only from experience. He is often credited with describing private property as a natural right, arising when a person mixes labour with nature. The phrase "long train of abuses" in the Declaration of Independence is taken from the Second Treatise.
john-magufuli: John Pombe Joseph Magufuli was born on 29 October 1959 in north-western Tanzania, then Tanganyika, on the shores of Lake Victoria, into a poor family. As a boy he looked after cattle and sold milk and fish to help support them. He attended Chato Primary School from 1967 to 1974, then Katoke Seminary, Lake Secondary School and Mkwawa High School. He earned a Bachelor of Science in education from the University of Dar es Salaam in 1988, majoring in chemistry and mathematics, and a master's degree in chemistry in 1994 and a doctorate in 2009 at the same university.

He taught chemistry and mathematics at Sengerema Secondary School in 1982 and 1983, then worked as an industrial chemist for the Nyanza Cooperative Union Limited from 1989 to 1995. In 1995 he was elected a Member of Parliament for Chato and served as Deputy Minister of Works until 2000, when he became Minister of Works. From January 2006 he was Minister of Lands and Human Settlement, from 2008 to 2010 Minister of Livestock and Fisheries, and from 2010 to 2015 Minister of Works again.

The ruling party Chama Cha Mapinduzi nominated him as its presidential candidate on 12 July 2015. He won the election of October 2015 with 58 per cent of the vote, with Samia Suluhu as running mate, and was sworn in as president on 5 November 2015. He was re-elected in 2020. Magufuli died on 17 March 2021 and was succeeded by his vice-president, Samia Suluhu.
john-maynard-keynes: John Maynard Keynes was born in Cambridge on 5 June 1883 into an upper-middle-class family. His father, John Neville Keynes, was an economist and lecturer in moral sciences at the University of Cambridge, and his mother, Florence Ada Keynes, was a social reformer who became the town's second female mayor. He studied at King's College, Cambridge, graduating in 1904 in mathematics. In October 1906 he became a clerk in the India Office but resigned in 1908 to return to Cambridge and work on probability theory. He became a fellow of King's College in 1909.

In the First World War the British government sought his advice. A few days before hostilities began he went to London at its request and helped persuade the Chancellor, Lloyd George, not to suspend specie payments. At the Versailles peace conference he tried to stop German reparations being set so high that they would damage Germany's ability to pay and buy exports, and so harm the wider world economy; the experience shaped his outlook, though he was unsuccessful. In the 1920s he published A Treatise on Probability and criticised the return to the gold standard in 1925 at the pre-war valuation.

During the Great Depression he challenged the neoclassical view that free markets would automatically provide full employment. He argued that aggregate demand determined the level of economic activity and that inadequate demand could cause prolonged unemployment, and he advocated fiscal and monetary policy to counter recessions. He set out these ideas in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, published in early 1936. In How to Pay for the War, published in 1940, he proposed financing the war through higher taxation and compulsory saving rather than deficit spending. He received a hereditary peerage in 1942 and helped to design the new international economic institutions, though the American delegation overruled him on several points.

Keynes suffered a series of heart attacks in 1946, beginning during the negotiations over the Anglo-American loan in Savannah, Georgia. He died at Tilton, his farmhouse near Firle in East Sussex, on 21 April 1946, aged 62. By the late 1930s leading Western economies had begun adopting his recommendations, and almost all capitalist governments had done so within two decades of his death. His influence waned in the 1970s, amid stagflation and criticism from Milton Friedman and other monetarists.
john-of-the-cross: John of the Cross was born Juan de Yepes y Álvarez at Fontiveros, a town of about 2,000 people near Ávila. His father, Gonzalo, a weaver who had been rejected by his family for marrying below him, died around 1545, and the family lived in poverty. His mother, Catalina, moved with her sons to Medina del Campo in 1551, where John entered a school for 160 poor children and later studied the humanities at a Jesuit school from 1559 to 1563. In 1563 he entered the Carmelite Order, and in 1564 he enrolled at Salamanca to study theology and philosophy. He was ordained a priest in 1567.

In Medina del Campo in 1567 John met Teresa of Ávila, who persuaded him to delay joining the Carthusian order and to follow her reform, which sought to restore the Primitive Rule of the Carmelite Order. On 28 November 1568 he founded a monastery for friars at Duruelo and took the name John of the Cross. After tensions among the Carmelites, a General Chapter at Piacenza in 1576 ordered the suppression of the Discalced houses.

On the night of 2 December 1577 Carmelites opposed to reform seized John in Ávila and took him to Toledo, where a court of friars sentenced him to imprisonment. He was lashed publicly at least weekly and held in a cell barely 10 by 6 feet. There he composed a great part of the Spiritual Canticle, and he escaped through a small window on 15 August 1578.

In 1580 Pope Gregory XIII authorised the separation of the Discalced Carmelites. John became a leader of the new order and in 1585 Vicar Provincial of Andalusia, founding seven monasteries there. After disagreeing with the order's leadership he was sent to La Peñuela in June 1591, fell ill and died of erysipelas at Úbeda on 14 December 1591. He was beatified in 1675, canonized in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926.

John's poems add up to fewer than 2,500 verses, and his theological works are largely commentaries on them. The Spiritual Canticle, in which the bride, representing the soul, searches for the bridegroom, Christ, is seen as a free Spanish version of the Song of Songs; its first 31 stanzas date from 1578, and it survives in versions of 39 and 40 stanzas. The Dark Night narrates the soul's journey to union with God through detachment, and the Ascent of Mount Carmel, composed between 1581 and 1585, is a systematic study of that ascetical path. His works were first published in 1618, and his writing influenced T. S. Eliot, Thérèse de Lisieux and Thomas Merton.
john-stuart-mill: Mill was born at 13 Rodney Street in Pentonville, then on the edge of London, the eldest son of Harriet Barrow and the Scottish philosopher James Mill. His father educated him, with the advice of Jeremy Bentham and Francis Place, and deliberately shielded him from children other than his siblings, aiming to create a genius intellect that would carry on the cause of utilitarianism. John Stuart was taught Greek at three, and by eight he had read Aesop's Fables, Xenophon's Anabasis and the whole of Herodotus, and had been taught arithmetic, physics and astronomy.

From 1823, at seventeen, until 1858 Mill worked for the East India Company. In 1836 he was promoted to its political department, handling correspondence with the princely states, and in 1856 he became Examiner of Indian Correspondence. When the Crown moved to take direct control of the Company's territories he defended Company rule and declined a seat on the Council of India, citing disapproval of the new system. He defended what he called a benevolent despotism over peoples he regarded as backward.

On 21 April 1851 Mill married Harriet Taylor after 21 years of friendship, declaring on marriage that he repudiated the rights the law gave him over her. He called himself, in the cause of women's rights, chiefly an amanuensis to his wife, who died in 1858. A member of the Liberal Party, he was the second Member of Parliament, after Henry Hunt in 1832, to call for women's suffrage. He died of erysipelas at Avignon on 7 May 1873, aged 66, and was buried beside his wife.

In A System of Logic (1843) Mill held, against William Whewell, that laws are found by observation and induction and need empirical verification. On Liberty (1859) addresses the limits of the power society may legitimately exercise over the individual: the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over a member of a civilised community against his will is to prevent harm to others.

In Utilitarianism he defended the principle, drawn from Bentham and his father, that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness. In The Subjection of Women, published in 1869, he argued that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong and should be replaced by perfect equality. In 1850 he answered Thomas Carlyle's defence of slavery in an anonymous letter, and he supported abolition in the United States.
john-the-baptist: John is named in all four canonical Gospels. Only the Gospel of Luke tells of his infancy: he was the miraculous son of Zechariah, an old priest, and his wife Elizabeth, who was past menopause. The angel Gabriel is said to have announced his birth to Zechariah while he served in the temple at Jerusalem. Luke also states that John and Jesus were relatives, and on this account the Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran calendars place the feast of his nativity on 24 June, six months before Christmas. Some scholars think that John belonged to the Essenes, a semi-ascetic Jewish sect that expected a messiah and practised ritual baptism.

The Gospel of Mark introduces John as the fulfilment of a prophecy, a messenger sent ahead and a voice crying out in the wilderness. John wore clothes of camel's hair and lived on locusts and wild honey. He proclaimed a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sin and said that another would come who would baptise not with water but with the Holy Spirit.

Baptism was the central symbol of his movement. The majority of biblical scholars agree that John baptised Jesus, and several New Testament accounts report that some of Jesus's early followers had earlier followed John. The Gospel of Matthew has Jesus identify John as the Elijah who is to come, while the Gospel of John has John deny that he is the Christ or Elijah.

According to the New Testament, Herod Antipas had John executed around 30 CE, after John rebuked him for divorcing his wife and unlawfully marrying Herodias, the wife of his brother Herod Philip I. The Jewish historian Josephus also mentions John in his Antiquities of the Jews and states that Herod Antipas had him executed at the fortress of Machaerus.

Followers of John persisted into the second century, and some proclaimed him the Messiah. The Mandaeans, an ancient ethnoreligious group, regard him as their most important and final prophet. In Islam he is the prophet Yahya ibn Zakariya, and he is also honoured as a prophet in the Baháʼí Faith and the Druze faith. In Catholic martyrology he is the only saint whose birth and death are both commemorated.
john-wycliffe: John Wycliffe was born in the village of Hipswell, near Richmond in the North Riding of Yorkshire, though the date is disputed: it is conventionally given as 1324, while records suggest the mid-1320s or, according to one scholar, a date after 1331. He is known to have been at Oxford around 1345. The book On the Cause of God Against the Pelagians by Thomas Bradwardine shaped his views, as did the Black Death, which reached England in the summer of 1348 and which he mentioned often in later life. He became a priest in September 1351 and completed his bachelor of arts at Merton College in 1356. In 1361 he was Master of Balliol College.

In 1374 Wycliffe was part of a group that negotiated at Bruges for the English government with the envoys of Pope Gregory XI, which may have begun his connection with John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster.
