He then began to write tracts and longer works. In De civili dominio he attacked the temporal rule of the clergy, the collection of annates, indulgences and simony. His theory of dominion held that the Church should not own property and that men in mortal sin could not exercise authority in Church or state, and he insisted on the poverty of all clergy.

In the summer of 1381 he set out his doctrine of the Lord's Supper in twelve short sentences, and the chancellor of the University of Oxford had some of them pronounced heretical. Wycliffe appealed to the king. Once he dismissed the doctrine of transubstantiation, he lost the support of John of Gaunt and many others. In his last years he argued that Scripture was the authoritative centre of Christianity, that the claims of the papacy were unhistorical, and that monasticism was corrupt.

Wycliffe withdrew to Lutterworth, where he sent out tracts against the monks and Pope Urban VI and left his last work, the Opus evangelicum, unfinished. He suffered a stroke while saying Mass on 28 December 1384 and died a few days later. Tradition credits him with a Middle English translation of the Vulgate Bible, now called Wycliffe's Bible, completed before 1384 and revised by John Purvey in 1388 and 1395, but more recent scholars suggest he had at most a minor part. His followers, called Lollards by their opponents, adopted many of his views, and his Latin writings greatly influenced the reformer Jan Hus.
johor: Johor covers nearly 19,166 square kilometres in the south of the Malay Peninsula, with the South China Sea to the east, the Straits of Johor to the south and the Straits of Malacca to the west. Tanjung Piai is the southernmost point of mainland Eurasia. The landscape is flat, broken by inselbergs and massifs, with Mount Ledang the highest point, and its tropical rainforests include the Endau-Rompin National Park. The area was known to people in Siam as Gangganu or Ganggayu, meaning Treasury of Gems, and Arab traders called it jauhar, from which the name Johor came. The Old Javanese Nagarakretagama called it Ujong Medini, land's end.

A bronze bell estimated to date from about 150 CE was found near the Muar River, and the lost city of Kota Gelanggi, known from an old Malay manuscript, is placed by some in the forests of Kota Tinggi District. After the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511, Ala'udin Ri'ayat Shah II, a son of Sultan Mahmud Shah of Malacca, founded the Johor Sultanate in 1528 by moving the court to the Johor River. It spanned the southern peninsula, the Riau Archipelago including Singapore and parts of Borneo and Sumatra, and fought a three-way contest with the Portuguese and the Aceh Sultanate.

After Mahmud Shah III died, the Dutch recognised one son as heir in 1818 and the British recognised the other the following year. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 established Johor's modern borders. Sultan Abu Bakar wrote its state constitution in 1895, and in 1914 it became a British protected state within the Unfederated Malay States. Japanese forces invaded in January 1942 after the Battle of Muar. Johor joined the Malayan Union in 1946 and the Federation of Malaya in 1948, and became part of independent Malaya in 1957 and of Malaysia in 1963.

Johor is a state of Malaysia and a constitutional monarchy headed by a sultan, with Johor Bahru as the state capital and Muar as the royal capital. It is divided into ten districts. The 2023 census counted 4,100,900 people, making it the second most populous state. Malay is the official language, Islam the state religion, and the population includes Malay, Chinese and Indian communities. Johor keeps a private army, the Royal Johor Military Force, which has protected its rulers since 1886. In 2008 the International Court of Justice awarded Pedra Branca to Singapore.
johor-bahru: Johor Bahru lies along the Straits of Johor at the southern end of Peninsular Malaysia, on mostly flat land with some hills, bordering Singapore. Its climate is equatorial, with steady temperatures, high humidity and an average annual rainfall of around 2,350 mm, and two monsoon periods each year. The name means New Johor in Malay, distinguishing it from Johor Lama, Old Johor. The area was originally Tanjung Puteri, a Malay fishing village, and the city has also been spelt Johore Bahru, Johor Baru or Johor Baharu.

In 1819 a dispute between the Malays and the Bugis split the Johor-Riau Sultanate: the mainland portion came under Temenggong Daeng Ibrahim, and the Riau-Lingga Sultanate under the Bugis. The Temenggong already had a close relationship with the British, who wanted to control trade at Singapore. By a treaty signed in Singapore on 10 March 1855, Sultan Ali was to be crowned Sultan of Johor and receive 5,000 Spanish dollars and an allowance of 500 a month, and in return ceded the sovereignty of Johor, except Kesang in Muar, to the Temenggong. The Temenggong renamed the territory Iskandar Puteri and at first administered it from Telok Blangah in Singapore, then, after he arrived in 1858, from the new settlement.

Under Sultan Abu Bakar the town was modernised from a fishing village, with administrative centres, offices, schools and a railway to Woodlands. The State Mosque and Royal Palace were built with the aid of Wong Ah Fook, a patron of the sultan. Abu Bakar set up his administration under a British style and a state constitution, the Undang-undang Tubuh Negeri Johor. Although the British had long been advisers to the sultanate, it did not come under direct colonial rule until the adviser's status was raised to that of a Resident, as in the Federated Malay States, under Sultan Ibrahim in 1914.

General Tomoyuki Yamashita's Japanese forces invaded the town on 31 January 1942. The British retreated to Singapore and blew up the causeway the day before. The Japanese used the sultan's Bukit Serene Palace as their base, aware that the British would not attack it. After the war Johor Bahru became a cradle of Malay nationalism, and UMNO was formed at the Istana Besar in 1946. The town remained the state capital after Malaysia's formation in 1963 and was granted city status on 1 January 1994.

Johor Bahru is the capital of the Malaysian state of Johor and had a population of 858,118 in the 2020 census. Its people are mainly Malays, Chinese and Indians, and it is part of Iskandar Malaysia. Its cultural sites include the Royal Abu Bakar Museum in the Grand Palace building and the Johor Bahru Chinese Heritage Museum, and the main football club is Johor Darul Ta'zim.
joint-stock-company: A joint-stock company is a business entity whose shares can be bought and sold by shareholders. Each shareholder owns stock in proportion, evidenced by certificates, and may transfer shares to others without affecting the continued existence of the company. It is an artificial person with legal existence separate from its members: it can own property, enter into contracts, and sue and be sued in its own name. In modern corporate law the form is often synonymous with incorporation and limited liability, so that shareholders answer for debts only up to the money they invested. The company is managed on behalf of the shareholders by a board of directors elected at an annual general meeting.

Finding the earliest joint-stock company is a matter of definition. The earliest records appear in China under the Tang and Song dynasties. The Tang developed the heben, with an active partner and one or two passive investors. By the Song this had grown into the douniu, a large pool of shareholders whose funds were managed by merchants called jingshang, with compensation based on profit-sharing.

In Europe an early form was the medieval commenda, usually used for a single commercial expedition. Around 1350 at Toulouse, 96 shares of the Société des Moulins du Bazacle were traded at a value that depended on the profits of the mills it owned, making it probably the first company of its kind. The Swedish company Stora has documented a transfer of an eighth of the company as early as 1288. The Hudson's Bay Company, the oldest corporation in Canada, received its royal charter from Charles II in 1670.

A corporation requires a legal framework that grants it legal personality and shields its owners from corporate losses, which also encourages new investors by making stock marketable. Where shareholders have limited liability, many jurisdictions require the company to publish annual financial statements so that creditors can judge its standing. Most of the largest businesses in the world are publicly traded companies whose shares are sold on a stock exchange, but most corporations are privately held, with no ready market for their shares.
jomo-kenyatta: Kenyatta was born with the name Kamau in the rural village of Ngenda, to Kikuyu farmers named Mūigai and Wambūi. The Kikuyu kept no birth records, so his date of birth is not known; one biographer suggested 1890 or 1891, while a fuller analysis suggested about 1897 or 1898. During the First World War he lived among the Maasai, adopting a beaded belt called kĩnyata, from which he took his name.

He joined the Kikuyu Central Association. In February 1929 he sailed to Britain to press the Kikuyu land question. He returned to Britain in 1931 and did not go back to Kenya for fifteen years, studying phonetics at University College London and social anthropology under Bronisław Malinowski at the London School of Economics.

Influenced by his friend George Padmore, Kenyatta embraced Pan-African ideas and co-organised the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester. He returned to Kenya in September 1946, farmed an estate at Gatundu and became vice-principal of the Koinange Independent Teachers' College. In 1947 he was elected President of the Kenya African Union, which lobbied for independence and drew wide African support but the animosity of white settlers. In 1952 he was among the Kapenguria Six, arrested and charged with masterminding the Mau Mau Uprising. He protested his innocence, a view later historians share, but was convicted. He was held at Lokitaung until 1959, then exiled to Lodwar until 1961.

After his release Kenyatta joined the Kenya African National Union in October 1961 and accepted its presidency. KANU won 83 of 124 seats in the May 1963 general election, and on 1 June 1963 he was sworn in as prime minister of the autonomous Kenyan government. In December 1964 Kenya was proclaimed a republic with Kenyatta as executive president. KANU's only rival, Oginga Odinga's Kenya People's Union, was prohibited from competing in elections.

By 1975, in the historian Maloba's words, he had in effect ceased to actively govern. In March 1975 the backbencher Josiah Mwangi Kariuki was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, after which support for the government eroded. Kenyatta died on 22 August 1978 and was succeeded by Daniel arap Moi.

He was called Mzee, meaning grand old man, and Father of the Nation, and a cult of personality surrounded him. His government pursued capitalist policies, expanded education and health care. Critics called his rule dictatorial and neocolonial, accused him of favouring the Kikuyu and of enabling corruption, and noted that Kikuyu still held most important government positions.
jordanes: Jordanes, also written Jordanis or Jornandes, was an Eastern Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent who became a historian later in life. His paternal grandfather Paria was secretary to Candac, a leader of the Alans who held Scythia Minor and Lower Moesia, a small client state on the Roman frontier. Jordanes himself served as notarius, or secretary, to Candac's nephew Gunthigis, also called Baza, a master of the soldiery of the Amali, the leading Gothic clan. He calls himself an unlearned man before his conversion. The nature of that conversion is obscure: it may have been from Arianism to the Nicene Creed, or it may mean that he became a monk or clergyman.

Jordanes wrote two works. The Romana is a history of Rome, written at the request of a certain Vigilius. The Getica, written in Constantinople about 551, interrupted the Romana at the request of a brother Castalius, who knew that Jordanes held the twelve volumes of the History of the Goths by Cassiodorus. Jordanes wrote an excerpt largely from memory, with his own knowledge and perhaps other material, and says he had only three days to review the work. He wrote in Late Latin rather than classical Latin.

The Getica opens with a geography of the north, especially Scandza, and begins the history of the Goths with the emigration of Berig in three ships from Scandza to Gothiscandza. The less fictional part begins when the Goths met Roman forces in the third century CE, and the work ends with their defeat by the Byzantine general Belisarius. With Isidore of Seville's Historia Gothorum, it is one of only two surviving ancient works on the early history of the Goths. Jordanes wrongly equated the Getae with the Goths, so that records concerning Dacians and Getae were attributed to Goths, and some scholars argue that he added fictional events, such as a Gothic war against Egypt.
jorge-amado: Jorge Leal Amado de Faria was born on 10 August 1912 on a farm in the village of Ferradas near Itabuna in the south of Bahia, the eldest of four sons. The village was then administered by the coastal city of Ilhéus, and he considered himself a citizen of Ilhéus. After a smallpox epidemic the family moved there when he was one year old. He attended high school in Salvador and by the age of 14 was writing for magazines and had helped found the modernist Rebels' Academy. His boyhood among the large cocoa plantations showed him the misery of workers living in almost enslaved conditions, a theme of several works, including The Violent Land.

Amado published his first novel, The Country of Carnival, in 1931, aged 18, and his second, Cacau, in 1933. His leftist activities made his life difficult under the regime of Getúlio Vargas: he was arrested for the first time in 1935, and two years later his books were publicly burned. Jubiabá won him a wide readership in France and was praised by Albert Camus. As a Communist militant he went into exile in Argentina and Uruguay in 1941 to 1942. He was later elected to the National Constituent Assembly for the Brazilian Communist Party with more votes than any other candidate in São Paulo.

After the party was declared illegal in 1947 he went into exile again, in France until he was expelled in 1950, and then lived in Czechoslovakia from 1950 to 1952. He won the Stalin Peace Prize in 1951. Back in Brazil in 1954 he left active politics and the party a year later, and gave himself wholly to literature. His second phase began in 1958 with Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon, which Jean-Paul Sartre called the best example of a folk novel. It turned in part from social realism to women characters and a smiling celebration of the traditions of Bahia. Its frank treatment of sexual customs scandalised Brazil, and for some years threats kept him out of Ilhéus.

Amado was elected to the Brazilian Academy of Letters on 6 April 1961 and held its 23rd chair until his death. He received the French Légion d'Honneur in 1984. His books have been translated into 49 languages, adapted for film, theatre and television, and he was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature at least seven times, from 1967 to 1973. He died in Salvador on 6 August 2001, four days before his 89th birthday.

The Fundação Casa de Jorge Amado, created in Salvador in 1987, protects his estate. The Casa do Rio Vermelho, the house where he lived with the writer Zélia Gattai, opened as a memorial in 2014, and the ashes of both are in its garden.
jorge-luis-borges: Borges was born on 24 August 1899 into an educated middle-class family in Palermo, then a poor area of Buenos Aires. His mother, Leonor Acevedo Suárez, worked as a translator and came from a family of criollo origin that had been much involved in the Argentine War of Independence. In 1914 the family moved to Switzerland, where he studied at the Collège de Genève, and travelled widely in Europe, including Spain. When they returned to Buenos Aires in 1921 he had little formal education and few friends, and he brought with him the doctrine of Ultraism. He began publishing poems and essays in literary journals and worked as a librarian and public lecturer.

Borges's father died in 1938. On Christmas Eve that year Borges suffered a severe head injury and nearly died of sepsis. While recovering he began exploring the new style for which he became known. His first story after the accident, Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote, appeared in May 1939, and his first collection of stories, The Garden of Forking Paths, followed in 1941, composed mostly of works already published in Sur.

Under Juan Perón, he was told he was being promoted from his post at the Miguel Cané Library to inspector of poultry and rabbits at a municipal market; asked why, he was told that he had been on the side of the Allies. He resigned the next day, and the Argentine Society of Writers held a dinner in his honour. In 1955 he was appointed director of the National Public Library and professor of English literature at the University of Buenos Aires. He was completely blind by the age of 55. In 1961 he shared the first International Formentor Prize with Samuel Beckett, and by the 1960s his work was widely translated. He was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

His best-known collections, Ficciones and El Aleph, appeared in the 1940s and explore dreams, labyrinths, chance, infinity, archives, mirrors, fictional writers and mythology. He never wrote a novel; he preferred the short story, finding that a novel required padding. He was also a notable translator from English, French, German, Old English and Old Norse, beginning at ten with a Spanish version of Oscar Wilde's The Happy Prince. He held that a translation may improve upon the original, and that different, even contradictory, renderings can be equally valid. He also practised literary forgery and the review of an imaginary work, a form he drew from Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus.
jorge-rafael-videla: Jorge Rafael Videla was born on 2 August 1925 in Mercedes, the third of five sons of Colonel Rafael Eugenio Videla Bengolea. His family was prominent in San Luis Province, where his grandfather Jacinto had been governor from 1891 to 1893. He entered the National Military College on 3 March 1942 and graduated in December 1944 as a second lieutenant. He became a brigadier general in 1971. In August 1975 President Isabel Perón appointed him General Commander of the Army.

After Juan Perón's death his widow Isabel became president amid violence, unrest and economic problems. Videla headed the military coup that deposed her on 24 March 1976. A junta took power, with Admiral Emilio Massera for the Navy and Brigadier General Orlando Ramón Agosti for the Air Force, and two days later Videla assumed the presidency. The junta called its rule the National Reorganization Process. It came to power during attacks by left-wing groups such as the ERP and the Montoneros and by right-wing death squads, and 293 servicemen and police were killed in left-wing attacks in 1975 and 1976.

The repression targeted guerrillas but also the church, unions, artists, intellectuals and students. According to human rights groups, thousands of Argentines disappeared in custody, with estimates as high as 30,000, many held in clandestine detention camps, and between 1,500 and 4,000 were thrown alive from aircraft into the sea. Children born to women prisoners were taken and given to military families, with their identities hidden. On the economy Videla left policy to José Alfredo Martínez de Hoz, who freed prices, exports and imports. Pope John Paul II opened mediation in 1978 in the Beagle conflict over islands at the southern tip of South America. Videla handed power to Roberto Viola on 29 March 1981.

Democracy returned in 1983, and in the Trial of the Juntas Videla was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment in 1985. President Carlos Menem pardoned him in 1990. He was jailed again in 1998 for the kidnapping of children, and in 2007 a federal court struck down his pardon. In December 2010 he was sentenced to life in prison for the deaths of 31 prisoners and in July 2012 to 50 years for the theft of babies, which the court said involved an estimated 400 to 500 children. He described himself as a political prisoner. He died on 17 May 2013 in a prison at Marcos Paz, an autopsy finding that he had slipped in a shower five days earlier.

The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo began their demonstrations on 30 April 1977, asking where their disappeared children were. In 1980 Adolfo Pérez Esquivel received the Nobel Peace Prize for reporting the abuses to the world.
jose-de-san-martin: José Francisco de San Martín y Matorras was born in Yapeyú, Corrientes, an Indian reduction of the Guaraní people, where his father Juan de San Martín was governor of the Yapeyú Department. The exact year of his birth is disputed, since there are no baptismal records, and documents point to either 1777 or 1778. The family moved to Spain in 1783, settling in Málaga. In 1789 he enrolled in the Regiment of Murcia as a cadet.
He fought in North Africa from 1791 and in the Peninsular War of 1808, and for his part in the Spanish victory at Bailén on 19 July 1808 he received a gold medal and promotion to lieutenant colonel.

In 1812 San Martín sailed for Buenos Aires and offered his services to the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. The First Triumvirate made him a lieutenant colonel of cavalry and asked him to form the Regiment of Mounted Grenadiers. His plan to defeat the Spanish forces menacing from the north by an alternative route through the Viceroyalty of Peru required a new army, the Army of the Andes, raised in Cuyo Province. He led it across the Andes into Chile.

At Chacabuco on 12 February the army won in a pincer movement; about 600 royalists were killed and 500 taken prisoner, against 12 dead in the Army of the Andes. San Martín declined the post of Supreme Director of Chile and proposed Bernardo O'Higgins, and he won at Maipú in 1818. He then sailed from Chile with a fleet on 20 August 1820 and landed at Paracas on 7 September. He was appointed Protector of Peru on 12 July 1821, and independence was declared on 28 July.

On 26 July 1822 San Martín met Simón Bolívar in two private meetings at Guayaquil. With no witnesses or minutes, their content can only be inferred from later actions and letters. San Martín then left Peru, resigned his command and moved to France in 1824. He settled in Brussels and died at Boulogne-sur-Mer on 17 August 1850. His remains were brought to Buenos Aires on 29 May 1880 and placed in a mausoleum in the Metropolitan Cathedral.

He was first acclaimed as a national hero by the Federals, while the unitarians resented his refusal to aid the Supreme Directors with the Army of the Andes. Bartolomé Mitre's biography made him universally acclaimed as Liberator of Argentina, though later historians corrected inaccuracies in it. His statues stand in most cities of Argentina and in Santiago and Lima, and the Order of the Liberator General San Martín is the highest decoration of the Argentine government.
jose-marti: José Julián Martí Pérez was born on 28 January 1853 in Havana, to Spanish parents: a Valencian father, Mariano Martí Navarro, and Leonor Pérez Cabrera, a native of the Canary Islands. He was the older brother of seven sisters. When he was four the family moved to Valencia, and two years later they returned to the island. In January 1871 he sailed from Havana to Cádiz and settled in Madrid, where he studied law and took part in debate on the Cuban question through the Spanish press, circulating documents that protested Spanish actions in Cuba.

Martí lived in Mexico City from 1875 and joined the editorial staff of the Revista Universal. In 1881, after a brief stay in New York, he founded the Revista Venezolana in Caracas, which angered the dictator Antonio Guzmán Blanco and forced his return to New York. There he joined General Calixto García's committee of Cuban exiles and worked as a journalist for La Nación of Buenos Aires and Central American papers. He translated novels, served as consul for Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay, and founded the newspaper Patria, which became the organ of the Cuban Revolutionary Party. In a letter to Máximo Gómez in 1882 he proposed a revolutionary party, to keep Cuba from falling back on the Home Rule Party after the Pact of Zanjón.

In 1891 he published the essay Nuestra América and, in October, the verses Versos Sencillos. In January 1895 United States authorities stopped three ships at Fernandina in Florida and confiscated weapons, ruining the Fernandina Plan. The uprising began on 24 February 1895, and a month later Martí and Gómez issued the Manifesto of Montecristi.

Martí was killed fighting Spanish troops at the Battle of Dos Ríos, near the confluence of the Contramaestre and Cauto rivers, on 19 May 1895. Gómez had judged the Spanish position strong and ordered his men to disengage, but Martí, seeing a young courier, called for a charge. He wore a black jacket and rode a white horse. He was buried at Santa Ifigenia Cemetery in Santiago de Cuba.

He wrote poems, essays, a serialized novel, lectures, letters and a children's magazine, La Edad de Oro, and is counted a major figure of the Spanish American movement known as Modernismo. His prose influenced Rubén Darío. Verses from Versos Sencillos were adapted into the song Guantanamera. Martí opposed slavery, warned of United States designs on Cuba and argued that Latin American countries should build institutions fitted to their own history and nature. His thought has been invoked in competing visions of the Cuban nation, and José Martí International Airport in Havana bears his name.
jose-mujica: José Alberto Mujica Cordano was born on 20 May 1935 in the Paso de la Arena neighbourhood of Montevideo. His father, a farmer, went bankrupt and died in 1940, when José was five. In 1956 he met the politician Enrique Erro, and he became general secretary of the National Party. In 1962 he and Erro left it to found the left-wing Unión Popular with the Socialist Party; its candidate for president received only 2.3 per cent of the vote.

In the mid-1960s Mujica joined the MLN-Tupamaros, a far-left armed group inspired by the Cuban Revolution. In 1969 he led one of six squads in the brief taking of the town of Pando, and in March 1970 he was shot six times while resisting arrest in a Montevideo bar. He was captured four times and twice escaped from Punta Carretas Prison, in September 1971 with more than 100 other Tupamaros through a tunnel, and again in April 1972. After the military coup of 1973 he was among nine Tupamaros held in squalid conditions, including more than two years confined in an emptied horse trough. He was freed in 1985 under an amnesty after democracy returned.

With other former Tupamaros he helped form the Movement of Popular Participation, which joined the Broad Front coalition. He was elected deputy in 1994 and senator in 1999, and served as minister of livestock, agriculture and fisheries from 2005 to 2008 under Tabaré Vázquez. In 2009 he won the Broad Front's primary and then the presidency, with more than 52 per cent in the runoff of 29 November, and took office on 1 March 2010.

His government legalised state-controlled sales of marijuana from 2012, saying that this would take the trade from drug traffickers, and it passed same-sex marriage and legalised abortion. Social spending rose from 60.9 to 75.5 per cent of public expenditure between 2004 and 2013, the minimum wage was raised from 4,800 to 10,000 pesos and trade unions were strengthened. In 2013 he spoke to the United Nations General Assembly, urging a return to simplicity. He gave about 90 per cent of his salary to charity, declined the presidential palace and drove a 1987 Volkswagen Beetle. The constitution barred immediate re-election, and Vázquez succeeded him on 1 March 2015. Mujica remained a senator until 2020, and he died at his farmhouse near Montevideo on 13 May 2025.
jose-rizal: José Protasio Rizal Mercado y Alonso Realonda was born on 19 June 1861. His family took Rizal as a second surname after Governor-General Narciso Clavería decreed in 1849 that Filipinos adopt Spanish surnames from a list, and continued to use Mercado. The family's patrilineal line traced back to Lam-co, a Chinese merchant from Fujian who settled in Calamba in 1697.

In May 1882, without his parents' knowledge, but secretly supported by his brother Paciano and his uncle Antonio, he left for Spain to study. He became an ophthalmologist by profession and a key member of the Propaganda Movement of the 1880s, which advocated political reforms for the colony.

Rizal wrote mostly in Spanish. His essays include El amor patrio of 1882 and Filipinas dentro de cien años, 1889–90, and he annotated Antonio de Morga's Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas, published in 1890 after he moved from Paris to Brussels. His novels Noli Me Tángere (1887) and its sequel El filibusterismo (1891) are together taken as a national epic. His poetry includes Mi último adiós, written in 1896.

On his return to Manila in 1892 he formed La Liga Filipina, which advocated moderate social reforms through legal means but was disbanded by the governor. On 6 July 1892 he was arrested for alleged possession of a seditious document and banished to Dapitan on Mindanao. There he built a school, a hospital and a water supply system, taught, and farmed. In February 1895 he met Josephine Bracken, an Irish woman from Hong Kong, who later became his common-law wife.

With Governor General Ramón Blanco's leave to serve as a doctor in Cuba, Rizal left Dapitan on 1 August 1896. By then the Katipunan's rebellion had become a nationwide revolution. At a stopover in Barcelona he was arrested on 6 October 1896. He was executed for rebellion on 30 December 1896 by a squad of Filipino soldiers of the Spanish Army, with a backup force of regular troops ready to shoot the executioners if they refused orders. Though not involved in the revolution's planning or conduct, he ultimately approved of its goals. His last words were reported as consummatum est, it is finished.

Rizal is widely considered one of the most influential figures in the Philippines and has been recommended as a national hero by an officially empaneled National Heroes Committee. No law, executive order or proclamation has officially proclaimed any Filipino historical figure a national hero.
joseph-bonaparte: Joseph was born Giuseppe Buonaparte on 7 January 1768 at Corte, then capital of the Corsican Republic, to Carlo Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino. Corsica was invaded by France in the year of his birth. He trained as a lawyer, sat in the Council of Five Hundred and served as French ambassador to the Papal States. In 1799 he helped Napoleon overthrow the Directory, and on 30 September 1800 he signed the Treaty of Mortefontaine, a treaty of friendship and commerce between France and the United States.

After Austerlitz, Napoleon declared on 27 December 1805 that Ferdinand IV of Naples had forfeited his kingdom. Joseph nominally commanded the invading army, with Marshal Masséna in effective command. The French crossed the border on 8 February 1806 with little resistance, and Joseph entered Naples on 15 February. On 30 March Napoleon decreed him King of Naples and Sicily. He kept most Bourbon officials in post and began reforms on the French model: monastic orders were suppressed and their property nationalised, feudal privileges and taxes were abolished with compensation for the nobility, and roads and public works were begun.

Joseph was moved to Spain in August 1808, and his brother-in-law Joachim Murat succeeded him in Naples. In Spain he was extremely unpopular, and his opponents called him Pepe Botella for alleged heavy drinking, though he was abstemious. His arrival sparked a great revolt and the Peninsular War, and his command of the French forces was largely nominal. He ended the Spanish Inquisition, but his foreign birth kept most Spanish people from accepting him. He left the throne after the French defeat at Vitoria in 1813.

After 1815 Joseph went to the United States, and from 1817 to 1832 lived mainly there, at Point Breeze, an estate at Bordentown, New Jersey. He was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 1823. He moved to London in 1832 and died in Florence on 28 July 1844. His body was returned to France and buried in Les Invalides. Joseph Bonaparte Gulf in Australia is named after him.
joseph-conrad: Conrad was born on 3 December 1857 in Berdychiv, in what was then the Russian Empire, in a region that had once belonged to the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland. He was the only child of Apollo Korzeniowski, a writer, translator, political activist and would-be revolutionary, and his wife Ewa Bobrowska. Almost all the countryside around was owned by the Polish nobility, to which his family belonged, and Polish patriotic literature was held in high esteem there. He was officially a Russian subject until his naturalisation as a British subject.

Conrad spoke Polish and French fluently from childhood and acquired English only in his twenties, always speaking it with a strong foreign accent. He served in the French and British merchant navies, and a Corsican seaman he befriended in Marseille, Dominique Cervoni, inspired some of his characters, such as the title character of Nostromo in 1904. In the autumn of 1889 he began his first novel, Almayer's Folly, published in 1895. His later novels include Heart of Darkness in 1899, Lord Jim in 1900, The Secret Agent in 1907 and Under Western Eyes in 1911.

Many of his novels and stories have nautical settings and depict crises of human individuality in what he saw as an indifferent, inscrutable and amoral world. He is considered a literary impressionist by some and an early modernist by others. Writing near the peak of the British Empire, he drew on the experience of Poland, divided among three empires, to explore imperialism and colonialism. In 1975 the Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe called him a thoroughgoing racist, a charge that most later criticism of Conrad has addressed.

Conrad was in Poland with his family when the First World War broke out in 1914, and they took refuge in the mountain resort of Zakopane. He died on 3 August 1924 at his house in Bishopsbourne, Kent, probably of a heart attack, and was buried at Canterbury Cemetery. His friends included Henry James, John Galsworthy, Stephen Crane and H. G. Wells. After the publication of Chance in 1913 he was the subject of more discussion and praise than any other English writer of the time, and his narrative style and anti-heroic characters have influenced numerous authors.
joseph-de-maistre: Joseph de Maistre was born on 1 April 1753 at Chambéry in the Duchy of Savoy, then part of the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia. His family was of French and Italian origin. Maistre was the eldest of ten surviving children and was probably educated by the Jesuits. After training in law at the University of Turin, completed in 1774, he became a senator in 1787, like his father. In his early years he was a liberal and a supporter of Gallicanism,.

The passing of the August Decrees on 4 August 1789 turned him decisively against the course of events in France. When a French revolutionary army took Chambéry in 1792 he fled. He found no position at the royal court in Turin and went to Lausanne, where he discussed politics and theology in the salon of Madame de Staël and began his career as a counter-revolutionary writer, with Letters from a Savoyard Royalist in 1793. After the French took Turin in 1798 he went to Venice and then to Cagliari, where the king of Piedmont-Sardinia held his court.

In 1802 he was sent as ambassador to Tsar Alexander I in Saint Petersburg. His diplomatic duties were few, and he became a well-loved presence in aristocratic and merchant circles and wrote his most influential works. After the restoration of the House of Savoy under the Congress of Vienna he returned to Turin in 1817 and served as magistrate and minister of state until his death on 26 February 1821.

In Considerations on France of 1796 he argued that the Revolution was divine punishment for the promotion of Enlightenment thought by the Ancien Régime. He held that constitutions are not products of human reason but come from God, and that written constitutions are scraps of paper. He criticised Rousseau and the Encyclopaedists for treating people as fundamentally rational and for resting theories on abstract reasoning instead of history. His book On the Pope of 1819 set out his religious view of authority: government must rest on grounds its subjects are not allowed to question, and in Europe the final religious authority lies with the Pope.

With Edmund Burke he is commonly regarded as a founder of European conservatism. His influence reached Juan Donoso Cortés, Charles Maurras and Carl Schmitt,. Isaiah Berlin called him the most brilliant and most polemical critic of the philosophy that underlay the French Revolution.
joseph-goebbels: Paul Joseph Goebbels was born on 29 October 1897 in Rheydt, near Mönchengladbach, to Catholic parents of modest means. As a child he had a deformed right foot that an operation failed to correct. He wore a metal brace, walked with a limp and was rejected for military service in the First World War. He aspired to be an author and in 1922 obtained a doctorate in philology from the University of Heidelberg. He took an interest in Hitler during Hitler's treason trial of 1924 and joined the Nazi Party that year, drawn largely by Hitler's charisma. He worked for Gregor Strasser in northern Germany as editor and speaker.

In 1926 Goebbels accepted the post of Gauleiter of Berlin. He answered only to Hitler and controlled the local SA and SS. He deliberately provoked street brawls for publicity and used large type and red ink on posters. In the Reichstag election of 20 May 1928 he was one of the first 12 Nazi members elected, which gave him immunity from prosecution. In 1930 Hitler appointed him Reich leader of Nazi propaganda in place of Strasser.

After Hitler became Reich chancellor on 30 January 1933, Goebbels' Propaganda Ministry quickly gained control over news, media, arts and information, and he used radio and film to full effect. He was an antisemite from a young age and repeatedly urged Hitler to act against Jews. He promoted persecution through propaganda, pogroms and legislation, and in Berlin he banned Jews from public transport and required Jewish shops to be marked.

In 1943 Goebbels began to press Hitler for measures to produce total war, such as conscripting women into the labour force. Hitler appointed him Reich Plenipotentiary for Total War on 23 July 1944, but his measures were largely unsuccessful. In April 1945 his wife Magda and their children joined Hitler in Berlin. Hitler killed himself on 30 April, and under his will Goebbels succeeded him as Chancellor of Germany for one day. On 1 May 1945 Goebbels and Magda killed themselves after poisoning their six children with a cyanide compound.
joseph-haydn: Joseph Haydn was born on 31 March 1732 in Rohrau, a village then on the border with Hungary. His father Mathias was a wheelwright and an enthusiastic folk musician, and his mother Maria, née Koller, had worked as a cook in the palace of Count Harrach. Neither could read music, but the family often sang together. Around the age of six he was apprenticed to a relative, Johann Matthias Frankh, at Hainburg, and later served as a chorister at St Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna. By 1749 his voice had broken, and after he snipped off a fellow chorister's pigtail he was dismissed and sent into the streets.

Haydn made his living as a freelancer, as a teacher, a street serenader and, in 1752, valet-accompanist to the Italian composer Nicola Porpora. He taught himself counterpoint from Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum and studied Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach. As Kapellmeister to Count Morzin he wrote his first symphonies, and in 1761 Prince Paul Anton Esterházy gave him a post that put him in charge of most of the Esterházy musical establishment; he became full Kapellmeister in 1766. Isolated at the palace of Eszterháza, he was, as he put it, forced to become original.

After Prince Nikolaus died in 1790, Haydn accepted an offer from the impresario Johann Peter Salomon to conduct new symphonies in London, leaving Vienna on 15 December 1790. Returning in 1795, he again served the Esterházys part-time, and with the librettist Gottfried van Swieten composed the oratorios The Creation (1798) and The Seasons (1801). In 1797 he wrote the Emperor's Hymn after hearing audiences sing God Save the King in London.

By the end of 1803 weakness, dizziness and swollen legs left Haydn unable to compose, though musical ideas, he said, pursued him to the point of torture. He died in Vienna on 31 May 1809 at the age of 77. He composed 106 symphonies, and the scholar James Webster judged that no other composer approaches his combination of productivity, quality and historical importance in the symphony and the string quartet. Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven are sometimes called the First Viennese School. The melody of the Emperor's Hymn was used for the Deutschlandlied of 1841, whose third stanza is the national anthem of Germany.
joseph-i-holy-roman-emperor: Joseph was born in Vienna on 26 July 1678, the eldest son of Leopold I from his third wife, Eleonor Magdalene of Neuburg. He was educated strictly by Charles Theodore, Prince of Salm, and became a good linguist. Perhaps through the influence of his formerly Protestant tutor, he was a less devout Catholic than his parents and an adherent of the early Enlightenment. His two enthusiasms were music and hunting. He was crowned King of Hungary at the age of nine, in 1687, and elected King of the Romans at eleven. His only military service was at the Siege of Landau in 1702.

As emperor Joseph reduced the large number of privy councillors, tried to make the bureaucracy more efficient and had some success in stabilising the chronically poor Habsburg finances. He continued the War of the Spanish Succession in an attempt to make his younger brother Charles king of Spain. Victories won by his general Prince Eugene of Savoy established Austrian hegemony over Italy. When he laid claim to imperial rights in Italy, he risked a military conflict with the Pope over the Duchy of Mantua, and Pope Clement XI threatened him with excommunication on 16 June 1708.

In Hungary he inherited the rebellion of Francis II Rákóczi, which lasted through his whole reign. Unlike his predecessors, he refrained from executing the leaders and agreed instead to a compromise peace, which in the long term eased the integration of Hungary into the Habsburg domains. In 1706 he confirmed the religious liberties of the Orthodox Serbs and Romanians. In 1710 he extended his father's edict of outlawry against the Romani: those who returned after entering the realm were to be mutilated or branded, adult men hanged without trial, and women and boys flogged and banished. Mass killings were reported as a result.

During the smallpox epidemic of 1711 Joseph became infected and died on 17 April at the Hofburg. He was buried in the Imperial Crypt, and the Vienna district of Josefstadt is named for him. He had married Wilhelmine Amalia of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1699, and their only son died before his first birthday. Under the Mutual Pact of Succession, his daughters were to precede those of his brother Charles, a ruling that made no provision for Charles's daughter Maria Theresa and led to the War of the Austrian Succession. Neither the Spanish war nor the Hungarian revolt was resolved in his lifetime.
joseph-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Joseph was born on 13 March 1741 in the Hofburg in Vienna, the eldest son of Maria Theresa and Emperor Francis I, and the brother of Marie Antoinette and Leopold II. He had 15 siblings. Tutors chosen by his mother gave him a structured education that included much history. In June 1760 he married Isabella of Parma, a granddaughter of Louis XV, in a match tied to the Austro-French alliance of 1756; they had a daughter, Maria Theresa. As co-ruler he sat on the State Council and wrote minutes for his mother that contain the germs of his later policy, favouring religious toleration, a weaker Church and relief of peasants from feudal burdens.

Maria Theresa's death on 29 November 1780 left Joseph free to pursue his own policy. He abolished serfdom in 1781, issued the Patent of Toleration that year giving limited freedom of worship, secularised church lands, made elementary education compulsory and, in 1784, ordered German to replace Latin as the language of instruction. He issued over 6,000 edicts and 11,000 new laws, and made German the compulsory language of official business, which especially affected Hungary. He refused to be crowned with the Holy Crown of Hungary, because he would have had to pledge to uphold its rights, and is known there as the Hat-wearing King.

In 1784 the Allgemeines Krankenhaus opened in Vienna, though centralisation worsened sanitation and caused a 20 per cent death rate in the new hospital. In foreign policy he twice tried to acquire Bavaria, in 1778 and 1785, and was thwarted by Frederick II of Prussia. He made an alliance with Catherine II of Russia in 1781, which drew Austria into the costly and largely futile Austro-Turkish War of 1787–1791.

Joseph fell ill in the autumn of 1788, probably with pulmonary tuberculosis, and died on 20 February 1790, just short of 49. He was buried in a plain copper coffin in the Kapuzinergruft in Vienna and succeeded by his brother Leopold II. His policies are known as Josephinism, and he was a patron of the arts who commissioned Mozart's Die Entführung aus dem Serail. Forged letters, the false Constantinople letters, long made him seem a more radical philosophe than he probably was.
joseph-stalin: Stalin was born Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili on 18 December 1878 (6 December in the Old Style calendar) in Gori, in the Tiflis Governorate of the Russian Empire. He was the third child of Besarion Jughashvili and Ekaterine Geladze, and the only one to survive infancy. His father's shoemaking workshop declined, the family fell into poverty, and Besarion became an alcoholic who beat his wife and son. In 1894 Stalin enrolled with a scholarship at the Tiflis Theological Seminary as a trainee Orthodox priest, but he lost interest, read Marx and attended secret workers' meetings. He left in April 1899. In November 1901 he was elected to the Tiflis Committee of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party.

After the October Revolution of 1917 Stalin joined Lenin's inner circle and became People's Commissar for Nationalities. After Lenin's death in January 1924 a struggle for the succession followed, in which Stalin used his post as General Secretary to place loyalists across the party and, with Kamenev and Zinoviev, formed a triumvirate against Trotsky.

From 1928 his five-year plans brought rapid collectivisation and industrialisation. State policy contributed to a major famine in the early 1930s, with Ukraine and Kazakhstan most affected. In the Great Purge of 1936–1939 at least 700,000 people were executed and over a million imprisoned in the Gulag. In August 1939 his government signed the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact with Germany, with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe. Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, and the Red Army captured Berlin in 1945.

After the war the Gulag system was expanded further, and by January 1953 three percent of the Soviet population was imprisoned or in internal exile. Stalin died on 5 March 1953 and was succeeded by Nikita Khrushchev, who denounced him and began de-Stalinisation.

Opinion of him remains divided. Most Westerners and anti-communist Russians view him as a mass murderer, significant numbers of Russians and Georgians regard him as a great statesman, and his regime has been widely condemned for mass repression, ethnic cleansing and the deaths of millions.
josephine-de-beauharnais: She was born Marie Josèphe Rose Tascher de La Pagerie on 23 June 1763 and was known as Rose until she met Napoleon, who first called her Joséphine. Her grandfather Gaspard-Joseph Tascher de La Pagerie was the first of an ancient French noble family to settle on Martinique, in 1726. Her father, Joseph-Gaspard, was a plantation owner and officer of the Troupes de marine who was almost always close to bankruptcy. Her mother's sugar plantation near Les Trois-Îlets was part of her dowry.

The name Joséphine de Beauharnais was not one she used herself. Beauharnais was the name of her first husband, Alexandre, which she gave up when she married Bonaparte, and the form arose under the restored Bourbons, who hesitated to call her by Napoleon's surname or her imperial title.

Alexandre de Beauharnais was guillotined during the Reign of Terror, and she was imprisoned in the Carmes prison until five days after his execution. In 1795 she met Napoleon Bonaparte, six years her junior, and became his mistress. They married on 9 March 1796, and on the certificate she reduced her age by four years and added eighteen months to his. In 1796 she began an affair with a Hussar lieutenant, Hippolyte Charles, and when rumours reached Napoleon his love for her changed entirely.

Napoleon became Emperor in 1804, and at the coronation at Notre-Dame on 2 December, after crowning himself, he crowned her empress. Shortly before, a quarrel at Saint-Cloud had nearly ended the marriage, for Napoleon felt pressed by his family over the lack of an heir. Her daughter Hortense reconciled them. The marriage was annulled on 10 January 1810 because she had not borne him a child, and he married Marie Louise of Austria.

After the annulment she lived at the Château de Malmaison near Paris, on good terms with Napoleon, who gave her a generous allowance and in April 1810 made her Duchess of Navarre. She died of pneumonia at Rueil-Malmaison on 29 May 1814. Napoleon, then on Elba, shut himself in his room for two days when he learned of it.

She bought Malmaison in 1799 and had it landscaped in English style, with a rose garden that she supervised closely. Napoleon ordered his warship commanders to forward plants from seized vessels, and Pierre-Joseph Redouté painted her roses for Les Roses, which was published after her death. She commissioned works from Antonio Canova. Through her children, Hortense and Eugène, she was grandmother of Napoleon III and ancestor of several European royal houses.
josephus: Josephus was born Yosef ben Mattityahu in Jerusalem, into one of the city's elite families. His father Matthias was a priest of the order of Jehoiarib, the first of the 24 orders of priests in the Temple, and his mother claimed descent from the Hasmonean dynasty. At about 26 he travelled to Rome to negotiate the release of Jewish priests imprisoned by Nero, and with help from Nero's wife Poppaea he succeeded. On his return, at the outbreak of the First Jewish–Roman War, he was appointed military governor of Galilee.

In Galilee Josephus fortified towns and contended with a rival, John of Gischala. He resisted the Roman army at the siege of Yodfat, or Jotapata, until it fell in 67. By his own account he was trapped in a cave with forty companions, who drew lots to kill one another, and he was one of two left who surrendered. He claimed to have predicted that Vespasian would become emperor, and Vespasian freed him in 69, whereupon he took the emperor's family name, Flavius. To many Jews his claims seemed self-serving.

He served Vespasian's son Titus as a translator during the siege of Jerusalem in 70, which ended in the near-total razing of the city and the destruction of the Second Temple. In 71 he went to Rome in Titus's entourage and became a Roman citizen and a client of the Flavian dynasty, with a pension. He wrote all his known works there. He read the destruction of the Temple as a sign that God had turned to the Romans because of Jewish sins.

His main works are The Jewish War, of about 75, Antiquities of the Jews, of about 94, a history of the world from a Jewish perspective, and his autobiography, the Life. Outside the Scriptures they are the chief source for Second Temple Judaea, with accounts of the Hasmonean dynasty, Herod the Great, the Sadducees, Pharisees and Essenes, and of figures such as Pontius Pilate, John the Baptist and James, the brother of Jesus. He is the first known source for the siege of Masada. Historians treat him with caution, since Carl Ritter held in the 1840s that his wish to bring his people honour among Greeks and Romans filled his history with distortions and exaggerations.

Christian readers prized him from the 4th century as an independent witness to the world of Jesus. Rabbinic writing almost never names him, and he was often seen as a traitor, until Kalman Schulman's Hebrew translation of 1863 revived Jewish interest. William Whiston's English translation of 1732 was among the books Christians most often owned after the Bible.
josip-broz-tito: Josip Broz was born on 7 May 1892 in Kumrovec, in the Zagorje region of Croatia, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. His father was a Croat and his mother a Slovene; he spent much of his early childhood with his Slovene grandparents but identified as a Croat. Conscripted in May 1913, he became a sergeant major at 22, the youngest in his regiment. Wounded and captured by the Russians in the First World War, he was sent to a work camp in the Ural Mountains and took part in the Russian Revolution. He met Pelagija Belousova in Omsk in 1918 and married her the next year.

Back in Croatia in 1920 he joined the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, outlawed on 30 December 1920. He was imprisoned in 1928, and Moša Pijade became his ideological mentor in Lepoglava prison. Released on 16 March 1934, he left Yugoslavia after King Alexander's assassination in October and worked for the Comintern in Moscow. In 1937, after the party's leader Gorkić was arrested and shot in Moscow, Broz became acting general secretary and built a younger leadership around Edvard Kardelj, Aleksandar Ranković and Milovan Đilas. Tito was one of several names he used while the party was illegal.

After the Axis invasion on 6 April 1941 he formed a Military Committee, and on 27 June the Central Committee named him commander-in-chief of the Partisans. A provisional government headed by Tito was assembled in Belgrade on 7 March 1945, and his People's Front won the elections of November 1945, which monarchists boycotted.

In 1961 Tito co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement with Gamal Abdel Nasser, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sukarno and Kwame Nkrumah, and became its first Secretary-General. From the 1950s his government let Yugoslav workers go to Western Europe as guest workers, and the constitution delegated much power to the republics. After the changes of 1974 he reduced his role in daily government but kept the last word on major policy. Critics call his rule authoritarian and point to the arrest of Milovan Đilas on 19 November 1956; others call him a benevolent dictator. He received 98 foreign decorations, and died on 4 May 1980.
jozef-pilsudski: Józef Klemens Piłsudski was born on 5 December 1867 into a family of nobility at Zułow, near the village of Zułowo in present-day Lithuania, then under Russian rule. He knew Lithuanian as well as Polish. The family was impoverished but cherished Polish patriotic traditions. Held at Irkutsk while being taken to Siberia, he was beaten with other political prisoners after a protest, and the cold of his first night in prison nearly killed him. In 1893 he joined the Polish Socialist Party, and in 1894 he became chief editor of its underground newspaper Robotnik. He remained a Polish nationalist and held that socialism and nationalism should be combined to win independence.

In the early 1900s almost all parties in Russian Poland sought autonomy within the empire, while Piłsudski's party was prepared to fight for independence. In 1906, with the connivance of the Austrian authorities, he founded a military school in Kraków for paramilitary units. On 3 August 1914 he formed the First Cadre Company in Kraków, and his Legions fought alongside Austria-Hungary against Russia. In 1917 he withdrew support for the Central Powers, and the Germans imprisoned him at Magdeburg.

On 11 November 1918 the Regency Council appointed him Commander-in-Chief, and that day he proclaimed an independent Polish state. As Chief of State until 1922 he faced a country with nine legal systems, five currencies and 66 types of rail system. From 1919 to 1921 he commanded forces in six wars over the borders. In August 1920 his plan, a counteroffensive led by a Reserve Army of about 20,000 men, repelled the Soviet advance at the Battle of Warsaw. On 14 December 1922 he handed his powers to President Gabriel Narutowicz.

After retiring in 1923, Piłsudski returned to power in the May Coup of 1926. The Sejm elected him president, but he refused the office and became Minister of Military Affairs, which he held until his death. His Sanation government sought to reduce the influence of parties and strengthen the army, and constitutional amendments of 2 August 1926 curtailed the Sejm. Its methods were at times authoritarian, and the imprisonment of opponents at Bereza Kartuska remains controversial. He died of liver cancer on 12 May 1935 at the Belweder Palace in Warsaw. He is widely regarded as a founder of modern Poland and a father of the Second Polish Republic.
juan-gines-de-sepulveda: Sepúlveda was born at Pozoblanco in the province of Córdoba, of humble background; his parents were Ginés Sánchez Mellado, a craftsman, and María Ruiz. In 1510 he enrolled at the University of Alcalá de Henares, where he studied philosophy and Greek, and in 1513 he began theology at the College of San Antonio de Sigüenza. In February 1515 he obtained a letter of recommendation from Cardinal Cisneros to the Spanish College in Bologna, where he matriculated that September. There he studied under Pietro Pomponazzi and gained a lifelong expertise in the works of Aristotle, encouraged by his patron Alberto Pío, Prince of Carpi, and by Giulio de' Medici.

By 1523 Sepúlveda had earned doctorates in arts and theology and had taken religious vows as a Dominican priest. When Giulio de' Medici became Pope Clement VII in that year, he served at the papal curia in Rome, where he gained a reputation for scholarship and rhetorical skill. He translated several works of Aristotle from Greek into Latin, among them the Parva Naturalia in 1522 and De mundo in 1523.

He also wrote on the religious controversies of the day: De fato et libero arbitrio against Martin Luther in 1526, De ritu nuptiarum in 1531 against the divorce proceedings of Henry VIII, and the Antapologia against Erasmus in 1532. He despised Luther, but respected Erasmus and corresponded with him for many years. In 1529 he wrote Ad Carolum V, urging Emperor Charles V to unite Europe and fight the Turks.

In Democrates, of 1535, Sepúlveda defended the idea that a just war based on natural law was compatible with Christianity. His case for the conquest drew also on Saint Thomas Aquinas, on the Roman law of just war and the right of conquest, and on the Bible, which he used to justify forced conversion; his position differed from that of the School of Salamanca represented by Francisco de Vitoria. He had never been to America. He claimed that some, though not all, Amerindians were natural slaves as Aristotle defined them in Book I of the Politics, and compared them to children before parents.

Bartolomé de las Casas used the same sources in reply. He held that Christianity should be offered to the natives as an option, not imposed as an obligation, and that no Amerindians lacked the ability to rule themselves. Sepúlveda's later works include histories of the deeds of Charles V, of 1556, and of Philip II, of 1564, and De regno, of 1570. He died on 17 November 1573.
juan-peron: Juan Domingo Perón was born in Lobos, Buenos Aires Province, on 8 October 1895, the son of Juana Sosa Toledo and Mario Tomás Perón. His father's family was originally Spanish but had settled in Sardinia, and his great-grandfather emigrated to Argentina in the 1830s.

Perón entered military college in 1911 and rose through the ranks. He supported the 1930 coup against President Hipólito Yrigoyen, a decision he later regretted. Between 1939 and 1941 he served as a military attaché in Mussolini's Italy, where he developed many of his ideas.

Perón took part in the 1943 revolution and became Minister of Labor, then Minister of War and Vice President, gaining a name for labour reforms. Political disputes forced him to resign in October 1945, and he was arrested. On 17 October workers gathered in the Plaza de Mayo to demand his release. He won the presidential election of 24 February 1946 by about 11% against an alliance of the Radical Civic Union and other parties, after he turned the United States ambassador's accusation of fascist ties into a choice between Perón and Braden.

His first term brought industrialisation, expanded social rights, tuition-free universities and, in 1947, votes for women, a measure tied to the work of his wife Eva Duarte. The government nationalised the Central Bank. It also fired dissidents, controlled the press and dismissed over 2,000 university professors. Several Nazi war criminals found refuge in Argentina. Perón was re-elected in 1951, but his second term began amid drought and a trade deficit. After conflict with the Catholic Church, pro-Church elements of the armed forces bombed the Plaza de Mayo in June 1955, killing about 300 civilians, and a coup deposed him.

Perón lived in exile in Paraguay, Venezuela, Panama and Spain while the Peronist party was outlawed. When the Peronist Héctor Cámpora won the 1973 election, Perón returned on 20 June 1973 amid the Ezeiza massacre and was himself elected president in October. Violence between left- and right-wing Peronists continued, and he could not resolve it. He died on 1 July 1974 and his third wife, Isabel Perón, succeeded him as vice president.

Supporters praise the Peróns for efforts to reduce poverty and dignify labour; detractors consider them demagogues and dictators. The movement continues mainly as the Justicialist Party. Perón was buried in La Chacarita Cemetery; in 1987 his tomb was desecrated and his hands stolen, a crime that remains unresolved.
juan-ponce-de-leon: Juan Ponce de León was born in the village of Santervás de Campos, in what is now the Spanish province of Valladolid. Early historians placed his birth in 1460, but more recent evidence shows he was likely born in 1474. The identity of his parents is still conjecture, but the historian Aurelio Tió argued that he came from a distinguished noble family, with Rodrigo Ponce de León, Duke of Cádiz, as his first cousin. In September 1493, aged nineteen, he sailed as one of 200 gentleman volunteers on Christopher Columbus's second voyage, which anchored off the island the Taíno called Borikén, later Puerto Rico.

In 1502 Nicolás de Ovando arrived as governor of Hispaniola. When the Taíno overran a Spanish garrison at Higüey in 1504, Ovando sent Ponce de León to crush the rebellion. He took part in the Higüey massacre, about which the friar Bartolomé de las Casas tried to inform the Spanish authorities. Ovando rewarded him by making him frontier governor of the province, with a land grant and an encomienda of Indian labour, and in 1505 he founded the town of Salvaleón.

In 1508 Ferdinand II of Aragon gave him permission for the first official expedition to Puerto Rico, which left Hispaniola on 12 July 1508 with about 50 men and found placer gold in the west of the island. He founded settlements near the mines at San Germán and Caparra, where local people were compelled to work under the encomienda system. The Crown named him the island's first governor in 1509. A long legal dispute with Diego Colón, Columbus's son, ended in 1511 with Colón replacing him.

King Ferdinand then urged him to seek new lands outside Colón's authority. A royal contract of February 1512 gave him the right to search for the islands of Beniny, and in March 1513 he set out from Puerto Rico with three ships at his own expense and sixty-five people. He named La Florida, charted the Atlantic coast to the Keys and north along the Gulf coast. The story that he sought a Fountain of Youth has no contemporary evidence, and most modern historians consider it a myth.

In 1514 Ferdinand knighted him and reinstated him as governor of Puerto Rico. In March 1521 he returned to south-west Florida with about 200 men, priests, farmers and artisans and fifty horses, the first large attempt to found a Spanish colony in what is now the continental United States. The Calusa attacked, and an arrow struck his thigh. The colonists abandoned the settlement and sailed to Havana, where he died in July 1521. He was buried in Puerto Rico, and his remains lie in the Cathedral of San Juan Bautista in San Juan.
judaea: Judea is a mountainous region of the Levant, part of which is desert, traditionally dominated by Jerusalem. It rises to 1,020 metres at the Hebron Hills, 30 km southwest of Jerusalem, and descends to as much as 400 metres below sea level in the east. Rainfall falls from about 600 millimetres around western Jerusalem to about 100 millimetres in the eastern parts, which form the Judaean Desert. Geographers divide it into the Hebron hills, the Jerusalem saddle, the Bethel hills and the desert east of Jerusalem. The main north-south route ran along the top of the central ridge.

The name is a Greek and Roman adaptation of the Hebrew Yehudah, the name of one of the Twelve Tribes of Israel and later of the Kingdom of Judah. The earliest known extra-biblical record of the name Judah is Nimrud Tablet K.3751, dated about 733 BCE. Under the Hasmoneans, the Herodians and the Romans the term covered a larger area than before. Josephus described Judea as lying between Anuath on the north and a village on the border of Arabia in the south, extending from the Jordan to Joppa, with Jerusalem in the middle.

According to the biblical account, a united monarchy under Saul, David and Solomon followed the settlement of the Israelite tribes, and scholarship is divided on the historical extent of such a kingdom. The northern kingdom fell to the Neo-Assyrian Empire in 720 BCE. Judah paid tribute to Assyria from 715, later to Egypt and, after 601 BCE, to the Neo-Babylonian Empire, until Babylonia conquered it in 586 BCE, destroyed the temple in Jerusalem and exiled many of the inhabitants. Cyrus the Great took Babylon in 539 BCE. Judea stayed under Persian rule until Alexander the Great's conquest in 332 BCE and later fell to the Seleucid Empire, until the revolt of Judas Maccabeus brought the Hasmonean dynasty, which ruled for over a century.

Under the Hasmoneans Jerusalem grew greatly, and the number of farming villages around it nearly doubled. Pompey besieged Jerusalem in 63 BCE during a civil war between Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, and political rule passed to the Herodian dynasty as client kings. Judea came under direct Roman rule in 6 CE. A revolt began in 66 CE, and in 70 CE Jerusalem was besieged and razed and the Second Temple destroyed. After the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132 to 136 CE most of the Jews in Judea were killed or displaced, and Hadrian renamed the province Syria Palaestina.

Judea's decline ended in the fifth century CE, when it became a monastic centre and Jerusalem a major Christian pilgrimage site. The Byzantines grouped it with Samaria and other districts as Palaestina Prima. The First Crusade took Jerusalem from the Seljuks in 1099.
judaism: The term Judaism derives from the Greek Ioudaismos, which first appears in the second century BCE in the book of 2 Maccabees. It meant forming part of a cultural entity, the opposite of Hellenismos, and the conflict between the two lay behind the Maccabean Revolt. According to the Hebrew Bible, God established a covenant with Abraham, who is presented as the ancestor of the Israelites. The Bible tells of a United Kingdom of Israel under Saul, David and Solomon, which split into the Kingdom of Israel and the Kingdom of Judah. Israel fell to the Neo-Assyrian Empire around 720 BCE, and Judah to Nebuchadnezzar II in 586–87 BCE. After the Achaemenid Empire took Babylon, many Israelites returned, and the Second Temple stood until 70 CE.

Judaism is an Abrahamic, monotheistic, ethnic religion. Religious Jews regard it as their means of observing the Mosaic covenant between God and the Jewish people. Its core texts are the Torah, the Nevi'im and the Ketuvim, which together make up the Hebrew Bible, or Tanakh. Alongside this Written Torah stands the Oral Torah, which includes the Mishnah and the Talmud. Rabbinic Judaism holds that God revealed his laws to Moses on Mount Sinai in both forms, and has been the mainstream form since the 6th century CE. The faith begins with ethical monotheism, the belief that God is one, which religious Jews express by reciting the Shema Yisrael twice daily.

Christianity was originally a sect of Second Temple Judaism, and the two religions diverged in the first century, at first over whether Jesus was the Jewish Messiah. Judaism's texts, traditions and values strongly influenced Christianity and Islam, and through Christianity it has had an indirect but significant role in Western culture. The Jewish Enlightenment of the late 18th century divided Western Jewry into the Orthodox, Conservative and Reform movements. Daniel Boyarin argues that Judaism does not fit conventional Western categories such as religion, ethnicity or culture.
juho-kusti-paasikivi: Paasikivi was born Johan Gustaf Hellsten on 27 November 1870 in Hämeenkoski, in southern Finland, to a travelling merchant from Tampere. His mother died when he was four, and his father died in debt when he was 14. He took the Finnish name Paasikivi in 1885, entered the University of Helsinki in 1890 and received a doctorate in law in 1902. He was Director-in-Chief of the Treasury of the Grand Duchy of Finland until 1914, and he sat in Parliament for the Finnish Party, which supported greater autonomy but opposed steps the Russians might perceive as aggressive.

After 1914 Paasikivi became chief general manager of the Kansallis-Osake-Pankki bank. After the Bolshevik October Revolution he championed full independence in the form of a constitutional monarchy. In the Finnish Civil War he stood on the side of the White government, and as prime minister from May to November 1918 he sought a German prince, Frederick Charles of Hesse, as king. With Germany's defeat the monarchy was dropped for a republic and his Senate resigned. In 1934 he became chairman of the National Coalition Party.

From 1936 to 1939 he was envoy in Stockholm, seeking Swedish defence guarantees, which did not come. Before the Winter War he represented Finland in the negotiations in Moscow and supported compliance with some of the demands. He led the armistice and peace talks, and resigned as envoy in Moscow when he learned that thoughts in Helsinki ran towards retaking lost territory with German aid. By 1943 he had concluded that Germany would lose the war.

Paasikivi became prime minister in 1944, and Parliament chose him president in 1946, at the age of 75, when Mannerheim resigned. His policy was realistic: he held that Finland must adapt to superpower politics and sign treaties with the Soviet Union, and he aimed to prove that Finland posed no threat to it. In spring 1948 he ordered army and navy units to Helsinki against a possible communist coup, and after the elections of that year he kept the communists out of government. His approach, called the Paasikivi doctrine, was named Finlandization in the 1970s.

He was re-elected in 1950 and opened the 1952 Summer Olympics in Helsinki. By the end of his second term the Karelian refugees had been resettled, the war reparations paid and rationing ended, and in January 1956 the Soviet Union removed its troops from the Porkkala naval base. He died on 14 December 1956.
jules-mazarin: Giulio Mazzarino was born on 14 July 1602 in Pescina in the Abruzzo region of Italy, the eldest of six children. His father, Pietro Mazzarino, had moved to Rome from Sicily in 1590 to serve as a chamberlain in the household of Filippo I Colonna, the Grand Constable of Naples. His mother, Ortensia Bufalini, came from a Roman family of noble origin. In 1628 he took a doctorate in both civil and canon law, and Pope Urban VIII, who forgave him for leaving his post in a papal regiment without permission, made him a papal emissary.

Mazarin offered his services to Cardinal Richelieu and moved to Paris in 1640. He advised Richelieu on political and cultural matters and carried out a diplomatic mission to Savoy, where he secured the position of the regent Christine, Duchess of Savoy, and arranged an alliance with France. He was made a cardinal on 16 December 1641. Richelieu did not name him as successor, though according to Mazarin he advised Louis XIII to employ him. After Louis XIII named three advisers, Mazarin and Léon Bouthillier, comte de Chavigny, had François Sublet de Noyers forced out in April 1643.

The long war against the Habsburgs cost a great deal, and Mazarin raised money by fines on Parisians living outside the old city limits, a tax on goods entering Paris and a levy on nobles who sat on royal courts and councils. Resentment of him and of the regent Anne of Austria led to the Fronde, which lasted from 1648 to 1653. The Parlement of Paris issued a charter forbidding new taxes without its approval. When the nobles' revolt led by Louis, Grand Condé, followed, Mazarin withdrew for a time to Brühl near Cologne, and returned to Paris in 1653 after Turenne had defeated Condé.

Between 1657 and 1660 Mazarin made an alliance with England, formed the League of the Rhine in 1658 and saw Turenne defeat Condé at the Battle of the Dunes. The Treaty of the Pyrenees, signed on 7 November 1659, added three provinces to France, and in 1660 he arranged the marriage of Louis XIV to Maria Theresa of Spain. He had also overseen the king's education from the king's eighth birthday and wrote guidance for him on government. He died on 9 March 1661.

Mazarin was a major patron of the arts. He founded the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture in 1648, introduced Italian opera to Paris and assembled a collection recorded after his death as 858 paintings and 128 statues, much of it now in the Louvre. He founded the Bibliothèque Mazarine, the first public library in France, and left funds for the Collège des Quatre-Nations, now the Institut de France.
julian-calendar: The Julian calendar was proposed in 46 BCE by Julius Caesar, from whom it takes its name, as a reform of the earlier Roman calendar, which was largely lunisolar. That calendar had 12 months and 355 days, with a 27- or 28-day intercalary month inserted between February and March in some years. The reform took effect on 1 January 45 BCE by Caesar's edict. To realign the year with the seasons, 46 BCE was made 445 days long: it already had 378 days through the regular intercalary month, and Caesar added 67 more by inserting two extraordinary intercalary months between November and December.

The calendar has normal years of 365 days and leap years of 366, in a cycle of three normal years and one leap year that repeats without exception, giving an average year of 365.25 days. The months were formed by adding ten days to the 355-day year: two extra days went to January, Sextilis and December, and one each to April, June, September and November. February stayed at 28 days, so the ordinary month lengths are those still used today.

The old intercalary month was abolished and replaced by a single leap day at the same point, dated the sixth doubled day before the Kalends of March, which gave English the word bissextile. The pontifices at first added a leap day every three years instead of every four, an error recorded by several ancient writers.

Caesar's reform applied only to the Roman calendar, but in the following decades many civic and provincial calendars of the empire were aligned to it, and it became the predominant calendar of the Western world for more than 1,600 years. Because the Julian year is longer than the solar year, the calendar gains one day every 128 years. By 1582, 21 March was ten days out of alignment with the equinox, and Pope Gregory XIII promulgated a revised calendar.

Most Catholic countries adopted it at once and Protestant countries over the following two centuries; Greece was the last to adopt it as its civil calendar, in 1923. Most Eastern Orthodox churches still base their liturgical year on the Julian calendar, as does the Berber calendar of the Maghreb.
julian-emperor: Julian, whose full name was Flavius Claudius Julianus, was born at Constantinople, probably in 331, into the family of the reigning emperor, Constantine I. His father was Julius Constantius, Constantine's younger half-brother, and his mother was Basilina, a Bithynian noble who died shortly after his birth. As the nephew of Rome's first Christian emperor, he was brought up a Christian. He was one of few in the imperial family to survive the purges and civil wars under his cousin Constantius II. His father was executed in 337, and he lived much of his life under Constantius's close supervision, though he was allowed to pursue an education in the Greek-speaking east.

On 6 November 355 Constantius appointed Julian Caesar of the West and married him to his sister Helena. Constantius meant him to be a figurehead, but Julian learned to lead an army in campaigns against the Germanic tribes on both sides of the Rhine. In 356 he recovered towns held by the Franks, including Colonia Agrippina, now Cologne.

In February 360 Constantius ordered more than half of Julian's Gallic troops east, which provoked an insurrection, and the soldiers proclaimed Julian emperor at Lutetia, now Paris. A civil war loomed, but Constantius died before the two met in battle, having named Julian as his successor. On 11 December 361 Julian entered Constantinople as sole emperor, and his first act was to preside over the Christian burial of Constantius.

Julian purged the top-heavy bureaucracy, openly promoted pagans to high office and tried to revive traditional Roman religion at the expense of Christianity. He expelled Christians from the military and forbade them to teach or study the classical texts. His efforts to build a Third Temple in Jerusalem were probably meant to harm Christianity rather than please Jews. The Christian tradition remembers him as Julian the Apostate. His reign saw a brief resurgence of paganism, but his policies had no lasting effect on its decline.

In March 363 he launched a campaign against the Sasanian Empire with the largest Roman army ever to face the Persians. After a victory outside Ctesiphon he moved into Persia's heartland instead of besieging the city, ran short of supplies and had to retreat while Persian skirmishers harassed him. He was mortally wounded at the Battle of Samarra and died on 26 June 363. His successor Jovian had to cede territory, including Nisibis, to save the trapped army.
